posts.title: How gyro instruments work
posts.headline: Two air-driven gyros share one engine pump; the turn coordinator runs on electricity, so it is the one to believe when the suction gauge reads low.
posts.alt: An X-ray view through the see-through instrument panel of a banking Cessna 172P: inside the attitude indicator's case a gold spinning wheel in two silver rings stays level, and the blue and brown horizon on the face stays level with it.
teaches: The attitude indicator's horizon stays level because its gyro, a heavy wheel spinning at about 18,000 RPM in two gimbal rings, holds its plane in space while the airplane pitches and rolls around it.

The heading indicator's gyro spins on its edge in a vertical plane, and its compass card, geared to the gyro, holds its direction while the airplane turns around it; it drifts slowly, so it is checked against the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes.

On the Cessna 172P one engine-driven vacuum pump draws air through a filter and across the rotors' buckets to spin both the attitude and heading indicators, and the suction gauge shows the suction, 4.5 to 5.4 inches of mercury in the 172P.
If that pump fails, both gyros slowly spin down and wander, and the 172P has no low-vacuum warning light, so a level airplane can look as if it is turning.

The turn coordinator runs on electricity and shows the rate of turn through precession: the turn's force on its rotor acts 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation and leans the gyro against a spring, more for a faster turn; with low suction, believe it rather than the attitude indicator.
posts.intent: Three of the six instruments in front of you hold a spinning wheel, and knowing what spins each one tells you which to trust when one fails.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Three of the six instruments in front of you in a Cessna 172P hold a gyro, a heavy wheel spinning very fast. In the attitude and heading indicators it resists being tilted, so the airplane moves around it. The turn coordinator uses a different trick, precession.

Two of them, the attitude indicator and the heading indicator, are spun by air from one vacuum pump on the engine. The third, the turn coordinator, is electric. So if the suction gauge reads low, believe the turn coordinator, not the attitude indicator.

article.heading: Why the horizon and the heading hold still
paragraphs: Inside the attitude indicator a rotor spins at about 18,000 RPM, revolutions per minute. That speed, with most of its weight at the rim, makes it hold its plane in space.

The rotor hangs in two hinged rings, called gimbals, one inside the other. When you bank or pitch, the airplane and the case turn around the rotor while the rotor stays put. The horizon bar is fixed to the gyro, so it stays level with the real horizon, and to you the horizon picture tilts in the case.
Just below, the heading indicator's rotor spins on its edge, in a vertical plane. Its compass card is geared to the gyro, so the card holds its direction while the nose swings around it.
It has no magnets, and a little friction in its bearings makes it precess, so it drifts slowly. Check and reset it against the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes.

figure.caption: The attitude indicator's gyro in its two gimbal rings (white), drawn see-through. The rings let the airplane pitch and roll around the wheel without tilting it.
figure.alt: A close view inside a see-through attitude indicator case: a gold spinning wheel held in two white rings, one inside the other, on a dark grid.

article.heading: One pump spins both
paragraphs: On the 172P a vacuum pump on the engine pulls air out of both instrument cases and vents it overboard. That draws cabin air in through a filter on the firewall and across little buckets cut into each rotor's rim, spinning it like a water wheel. A relief valve keeps the suction from going too high.

The suction gauge on the panel's left shows the suction. The 172P's handbook wants 4.5 to 5.4 inches of mercury. Outside that range, it says, the attitude and heading indicators should not be considered reliable.
If the pump fails, both gyros slowly spin down and wander. The 172P has no low-vacuum warning light, only the gauge, so a level airplane can look as if it is turning.

figure.caption: The vacuum system drawn see-through: the engine-driven pump, the filter and the air (light blue) on its way to both gyros. The hose routing is simplified. In the 172P, air comes in through the filter, spins both gyros and goes on to the engine-driven pump, with a relief valve on that line.
figure.alt: An X-ray view behind a Cessna 172P panel: the attitude and heading indicators with gold rotors, light-blue arrows of air at the black hoses, a white filter labelled Filter below and a labelled vacuum pump on the engine.

article.heading: Why the turn coordinator is electric
paragraphs: The turn coordinator is the third gyro. On the 172P it runs on the electrical system, so one failure cannot take all three. Its face says D.C. ELEC. In another airplane, check the handbook for what powers each gyro.

Its gimbal is angled up about 30 degrees, so it senses roll as well as yaw. When the airplane turns, it pushes on the spinning rotor's rim, and the rotor reacts 90 degrees further around, in the direction it spins. That tilts the gimbal against a spring, more for a faster turn. The little airplane shows your rate of turn, not your bank angle, and gives no pitch information.

article.heading: Three mistakes with the gyros
paragraphs: Trusting the vacuum gyros after the suction drops. Once the rotors slow down, the attitude and heading indicators wander, and the little horizon can show a bank that isn't there. Use the turn coordinator for turns and the magnetic compass for heading. Take pitch from the outside horizon, or from airspeed, altitude and vertical speed.
Waiting for a warning. Many small airplanes have no vacuum failure warning, so the suction gauge is your alarm. Check it in your scan.

Resetting the heading indicator in a turn or a climb. Set it on the ground, stopped or taxiing straight, or in straight and level flight at a steady speed. Otherwise the compass's own errors get copied in.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Why does the attitude indicator's horizon stay level when you bank?
2. What spins the heading indicator's gyro in a 172P?
3. The suction gauge reads 2 inches of mercury, the attitude indicator shows a gentle left bank, and the turn coordinator's little airplane is level. Which do you trust, and what else has failed?
4. Why is the turn coordinator electric?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Its gyro holds its plane in space and the horizon bar is fixed to it, so the airplane rolls around it.
2. Air from the engine-driven vacuum pump, the same pump that spins the attitude indicator.
3. Trust the turn coordinator. With suction that low, the attitude indicator and the heading indicator are both unreliable.
4. So a vacuum pump failure cannot take all three gyros at once.

posts.title: How magnetos work
posts.headline: Two engine-driven magnetos fire two plugs in every cylinder. OFF only works through a ground wire, so a broken one leaves a magneto live.
posts.alt: An X-ray view of the back of a Cessna 172P's Lycoming engine, its cylinders and wiring in grey, with the two gold magnetos ringed and labelled Magnetos and their spark-plug leads running forward.
teaches: The Cessna 172P's Lycoming O-320-D2J gets its sparks from two engine-driven magnetos on the rear of the engine, and a magneto makes its current independently of the airplane's electrical system, so the engine keeps running with the master switch off.
Inside a magneto a rotating magnet builds current in a coil; when the breaker points open, the coil sends a high-voltage pulse that jumps a spark plug's gap.
Each cylinder has two spark plugs and each magneto fires one of them, so if one magneto fails the other keeps every cylinder firing.

On the run-up check at 1,700 RPM the engine slows a little on one magneto because one spark plug per cylinder burns the mixture more slowly; the 172P allows a drop of up to 125 RPM on either magneto and up to 50 RPM between them.

Ignition OFF stops a magneto by grounding it through its own wire, the P-lead; if that wire breaks, OFF cannot stop that magneto and moving the propeller by hand can start the engine, and no RPM drop on the check may mean faulty grounding.
posts.intent: Your engine makes its own sparks, which is why it keeps running with the master off and why a propeller is never safe to touch.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A piston engine like the Cessna 172P's makes its own sparks. Two magnetos, driven by the engine, fire two spark plugs in every cylinder, and they need nothing from the battery or the alternator. That is why the engine keeps running with the master switch off.
The ignition switch stops a magneto by grounding it through a wire. If that wire breaks, OFF no longer stops that magneto, so you treat every propeller as if the engine could start.

article.heading: How a magneto makes a spark
paragraphs: The 172P's Lycoming O-320 carries its two magnetos on the back of the engine, where the engine turns them. Inside each one a magnet spins past a coil and builds up current in its first winding.

A small switch called the breaker points then snaps open, and that current stops all at once. The magnetic field through the coil flips fast, and a second winding of thousands of turns, wound over the first, turns that change into a high-voltage pulse. A rotating distributor sends each pulse down the lead to the right spark plug, where it jumps the plug's gap.

The magneto makes all of this itself, so once the engine runs, the battery and the alternator play no part in the sparks. The battery still matters for starting, because the starter only cranks the engine with the master switch on.

figure.caption: The breaker points, the small switch inside a magneto, drawn as a simplified schematic and shown open. Opening them is what makes the coil fire a spark.
figure.alt: A close view inside a see-through magneto: a small hinged steel arm swung away from its contact, labelled Points open, beside the spinning shaft, with gold magneto parts around it.

article.heading: Two plugs in every cylinder
paragraphs: Each of the four cylinders has two spark plugs, eight in all. On the 172P the right magneto fires the lower right and upper left plugs, and the left magneto fires the lower left and upper right plugs.

So each magneto fires one plug in every cylinder. If one magneto quits, the other keeps all four cylinders firing. That is the point of having two. Two flame fronts also burn the mixture faster than one, which is why the engine slows a little when only one plug fires in each cylinder.

article.heading: Three mistakes with the ignition switch
paragraphs: Skipping the return to BOTH. The 172P's Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) makes the magneto check at 1,700 RPM, engine revolutions per minute. Select R and note the RPM, then go back to BOTH to clear the other set of plugs. Then select L, note the RPM, and return to BOTH. The drop should not exceed 125 RPM on either magneto or 50 RPM between them.

Ignoring a check with no drop at all, which feels like good news but isn't. Turning the key to OFF connects each magneto to the airplane's metal frame through its own wire, the P-lead, which stops its sparks. Selecting one magneto grounds the other the same way. So if nothing changes when you select one magneto, the one you tried to switch off may still be firing. The POH treats an absent drop as a sign of faulty grounding, or of timing set to fire the sparks earlier than specified.

Trusting OFF on the ramp. If a P-lead breaks, OFF cannot silence that magneto. It stays live: it can still produce sparks when the propeller is turned, even with the key OFF. Moving the propeller by hand can then start the engine with fuel left in a cylinder. The POH says to treat the propeller as if the ignition switch were on and to stay out of its arc. A normal shutdown does not rely on the key alone. The POH pulls the mixture to IDLE CUT-OFF first, which stops the fuel and so the engine, then turns the ignition switch OFF.

The wire's route is illustrative; only its ends are sourced. Reel credits: 3D model “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified. Engine sound “1978 Cessna 172 Departure” by Wingspan Adventures & Flight (youtube.com), CC BY 3.0, modified.
figure.alt: A gold magneto with its green ground wire running down toward the cockpit, a red ring labelled Break where the wire is broken at the magneto, and an inset of the ignition key turned to OFF.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. You turn the master switch off in flight, so does the engine stop?
2. Why does the engine slow a little when you select one magneto?
3. On the run-up the RPM does not change at all when you select L, so what could that mean?
4. The key is OFF and in your pocket, so is the propeller safe to turn by hand?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. No. The magnetos make their own current, so the engine keeps running. You lose the airplane's electrical power, not the ignition.
2. With one magneto, only one plug fires in each cylinder, so the mixture takes longer to burn.
3. The right magneto may not be grounding, so it may still be firing. That is a fault to get fixed before flight.
4. No. A broken P-lead leaves a magneto live, so treat every propeller as if the engine could start.

posts.title: Density altitude, explained
posts.headline: On a 70°F day at a 5,883-foot field, altimeter 30.10, your airplane performs as if it's at about 7,700 feet.
posts.alt: Cover slide titled Density altitude. A small airfield in a high mountain valley: the house Cessna 172 climbs out over the runway toward rising, pine-covered ground under high peaks. Text: On a 70°F day at a 5,883-foot field, altimeter 30.10, your airplane performs as if it's at about 7,700 feet.
caption: You can't detect the effect of high density altitude on your airspeed indicator. On a 70°F day at a 5,883-foot field, altimeter 30.10, your airplane performs as if it's at about 7,700 feet.

You lift off and climb at your usual indicated speeds, but you're faster over the ground, with less power and thrust to get there. So you need more runway and climb at a shallower angle. Your landing roll is longer too. Work out your takeoff distance for today's conditions before you go. Taking off from a field above 3,000 feet? If your airplane's procedure calls for it, lean for maximum rpm in a full-throttle runup before takeoff. Send this to someone who flies from a hot or high field.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. It is the vertical distance above sea level in the standard atmosphere at which a given density is to be found.

Under standard conditions, pressure altitude and density altitude identify the same level. Regardless of the actual altitude at which the aircraft is operating, it will perform as though it were operating at an altitude equal to the existing density altitude.

Density altitude is a measure of air density. It is not to be confused with pressure altitude, true altitude, or absolute altitude, and it is not to be used as a height reference, but as a determining criteria in the performance capability of an aircraft.

The conditions that result in a high density altitude are high elevations, low atmospheric pressures, high temperatures, high humidity, or some combination of these factors. Lower elevations, high atmospheric pressure, low temperatures, and low humidity are more indicative of low density altitude.

Density is directly proportional to pressure: if the pressure is lowered, the density is lowered (at a constant temperature). Increasing the temperature decreases the density (at a constant pressure). Pilots can expect the density to decrease with altitude.

Temperature is the most important factor, since temperature has the greatest effect on density horizontally in the atmosphere. On hot days, the air becomes less dense, causing high density altitudes; on cold days, the air is denser, causing lower density altitudes.

Water vapor is lighter than air, so moist air is lighter than dry air: as the water content of the air increases, the air becomes less dense, increasing density altitude and decreasing performance. Humidity alone is usually not considered an important factor in calculating density altitude and aircraft performance, but it is a contributing factor.

In the handbook's humidity example, at 8,000 feet with a temperature of 80° and a dew point of 75°, the density altitude is 11,564 feet; with no humidity, the density altitude would be almost 500 feet lower.

As air becomes less dense, it reduces power because the engine takes in less air, thrust because a propeller is less efficient in thin air (there is less air for the propeller to work with), and lift because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils.

A pilot cannot detect the effect of high density altitude on the airspeed indicator. The aircraft lifts off, climbs, cruises, glides, and lands at the prescribed indicated airspeeds, but at a specified indicated airspeed, the true airspeed and groundspeed increase proportionally as density altitude becomes higher.

High density altitude lengthens the takeoff and landing rolls and reduces the rate of climb. Before lift-off the plane must attain a faster groundspeed and needs more runway, and the reduced power and thrust add a need for still more runway; at a prescribed indicated airspeed it flies at a faster true airspeed, which means climbing at a shallower angle.

An average small airplane requiring 1,000 feet for takeoff at sea level under standard atmospheric conditions will require a takeoff run of approximately 2,000 feet at an operational altitude of 5,000 feet.

Density altitude is determined by first finding pressure altitude and then correcting it for nonstandard temperature. The pressure altitude can be determined by any of the three following methods: by setting the barometric scale of the altimeter to 29.92 "Hg and reading the indicated altitude, by applying a correction factor to the indicated altitude according to the reported altimeter setting, or by using a flight computer. Using a flight computer, density altitude can be computed by inputting the pressure altitude and outside air temperature; it can also be determined from a density altitude chart.

In the handbook's density altitude chart example, an airport elevation of 5,883 feet with an altimeter setting of 30.10 "Hg reads -165 in the conversion column, so subtracting 165 feet gives a pressure altitude of 5,718 feet; at an outside air temperature of 70°F, the chart gives an approximate density altitude of 7,700 feet.

The pilot must make an accurate prediction of takeoff distance from the performance data of the AFM/POH, regardless of the runway available. The most critical conditions of takeoff performance are the result of some combination of high gross weight, altitude, temperature, and unfavorable wind.

Although an aircraft is certified for a specified maximum gross takeoff weight, it may not safely take off at this weight under all conditions: conditions that affect takeoff and climb performance, such as high elevations, high temperatures, and high humidity (high density altitudes), may require a reduction in weight before flight is attempted.

Maximum surface air temperature usually occurs during the midafternoon, and minimum surface air temperature usually occurs shortly after sunrise. Advancing or delaying a departure may reduce risk likelihood, and canceling a flight is necessary if the pilot cannot mitigate risk sufficiently by other means.
Any attempt to take off below the recommended speed means that the aircraft could stall, be difficult to control, or have a very low initial rate of climb.

In the handbook's case study, a takeoff at maximum gross weight from Animas Air Park (elevation 6,684 feet, where July temperatures result in a high density altitude) had a calculated takeoff distance of 4,700 feet, and the pilot's 20 percent safety factor produced a desired runway length of 5,640 feet, which exceeds the available 5,000-foot runway. She reduced the departure fuel load and had her passengers board at an airport with a 9,200-foot runway instead.

At airports with elevations of 2,000 feet and higher, control towers and FSSs broadcast the advisory "Check Density Altitude" when the temperature reaches a predetermined level; the pilot retains the responsibility to compute density altitude, when appropriate, as a part of preflight duties.
The handbook's sample takeoff distance chart notes that prior to takeoff from fields above 3,000 feet elevation, the mixture should be leaned to give maximum rpm in a full throttle, static runup.
posts.intent: In: what density altitude is (pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature; the airplane performs as if it were at that altitude); what raises it (high elevation, heat, humidity and low pressure); what it does to the airplane (less power, thrust and lift, so a longer takeoff roll and a shallower climb, flown at the usual indicated airspeeds but a higher true airspeed and groundspeed); how you work it out (pressure altitude from the altimeter setting, then the temperature, on a chart or a flight computer, through the handbook's own worked example); and what you do on a hot, high day (takeoff distance and climb from the airplane's charts, a margin, then less weight, the cool of the morning or a longer runway when it does not fit, and lifting off at the normal indicated speed). Out: reading takeoff and landing charts step by step (its own topic), turbocharging, and mountain flying technique. The 2026-09-11 single on the same subject (perf-density-altitude, headline 'Thin air lengthens your takeoff and flattens your climb.') is linked from the page, and no slide uses its headline.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature: the height in the standard atmosphere where today's air density would be found. Your airplane performs as if it were there, whatever its real altitude. It is a measure of air density, not a height to fly by. High elevation, heat, humidity and low pressure all raise it. A high density altitude means a longer takeoff and landing roll and a weaker climb.

figure.caption: The field's own elevation, and the higher level the airplane performs as if it were at on a hot day.
figure.alt: A valley airfield seen from the side under a mountain face. A white line along the runway is labelled FIELD ELEVATION; a dashed amber line higher up, with an arrow up to it, is labelled PERFORMS AS IF HERE.

article.heading: What raises it
paragraphs: High elevations, low pressure, high temperatures and high humidity all raise density altitude. Lower elevations, high pressure, low temperatures and low humidity point to a low one.

Temperature is the most important of the weather factors. Hot days make the air less dense, and cold days make it denser. Low pressure thins the air too, so an altimeter setting below 29.92 inches pushes density altitude up.

Humidity is a smaller factor. Water vapor is lighter than air, so moist air is less dense than dry air. In the handbook's example, at 8,000 feet with a temperature of 80° and a dew point of 75°, the density altitude is 11,564 feet. With no humidity it would be almost 500 feet lower.

figure.caption: A high field in hard afternoon sun: two of the four things that raise density altitude.
figure.alt: A Cessna 172 parked on the ramp of a high mountain-valley airfield in hard afternoon light, with bare peaks behind. Labels read 1 HIGH FIELD and 2 HOT AFTERNOON SUN.

article.heading: What it does to the airplane
paragraphs: Thin air takes power from the engine, because the engine takes in less air. It takes thrust from the propeller and lift from the wing.

You can't detect the effect on the airspeed indicator. You lift off, climb and land at the usual indicated airspeeds, but your true airspeed and groundspeed are higher. So you need more runway to get airborne, and the lost power and thrust add still more. At a given indicated airspeed you climb at a shallower angle, and the landing roll is longer too.
Take an average small airplane that needs 1,000 feet to take off at sea level on a standard day. At an operational altitude of 5,000 feet, it needs about 2,000.

article.heading: Working it out
paragraphs: First find pressure altitude. Set the altimeter to 29.92 inches and read it, correct the field elevation for the reported altimeter setting, or use a flight computer. Then correct it for temperature with a density altitude chart or a flight computer.

In the handbook's chart example, the airport elevation is 5,883 feet and the altimeter setting is 30.10 inches. The conversion column reads minus 165, so the pressure altitude is 5,718 feet. At 70°F, the chart gives about 7,700 feet.
At airports 2,000 feet and higher, towers and flight service stations broadcast "Check density altitude" when the temperature climbs. Working it out is still part of your own preflight.

article.heading: Three mistakes on a hot, high day
paragraphs: Run the numbers before you decide. Take the takeoff distance and climb from your POH whatever the runway length, then add a margin. Read the charts at the real pressure altitude and temperature, with your weight and today's wind. Allow for the runway's slope and surface too. Being certified for a maximum gross weight doesn't mean you can take off at it today.

Change the plan when the numbers don't fit. Take less weight, use a longer runway or go when it's cooler. The day's lowest temperature usually comes shortly after sunrise, and the highest in the midafternoon. If none of that is enough, don't go.

Lift off at the recommended speed, not before it. Below that speed the airplane could stall, be hard to control or climb very slowly. Lean as your POH says. The handbook's sample takeoff chart, for one airplane, leans for maximum rpm in a full-throttle static runup before takeoff from fields above 3,000 feet.

figure.alt: A Cessna 172 on the runway of the same airfield just after sunrise, the sun clearing the peaks on the left, labelled USUALLY THE DAY'S COOLEST.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for what?
2. Which weather factor matters most to density altitude?
3. Why does a high density altitude lengthen the takeoff roll when you still lift off at the usual indicated airspeed?
4. Your takeoff distance is 4,700 feet, you add a 20 percent margin and the runway is 5,000 feet, so do you go?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. Nonstandard temperature, once you have the pressure altitude.
2. Temperature, because hot days make the air less dense.
3. Your true airspeed and groundspeed are higher at that indicated airspeed, and the engine and propeller give you less power and thrust to reach it.
4. Not like that, because 4,700 feet plus 20 percent is 5,640 feet. Take less weight, use a longer runway or wait for cooler air, and if it still doesn't fit, don't go.

posts.title: How the pitot tube works
posts.headline: Block the tube's front with its drain clear and the needle reads zero. Seal the drain too and it acts like an altimeter.
posts.alt: The 172P's airspeed indicator over a Cessna 172 climbing in grey cloud. The needle points at 158 on the red line, which is ringed in white, beside the gold label 158 KT and RED LINE, while a glowing cyan outline needle labelled 70 KT marks the airplane's real speed. Not to scale.
teaches: On the Cessna 172P the pitot tube is mounted on the lower surface of the left wing and the static port on the lower left side of the forward fuselage, and the airspeed indicator needs both.

Pressure from the pitot tube fills a diaphragm inside the airspeed indicator, the case around it is kept at static (outside) pressure from the static port, and the needle shows the difference, the dynamic pressure that grows with speed.

Moisture including ice, dirt or insects can block the tube; at Brisbane Airport, mud-nesting keyhole wasps fully blocked 3D-printed replica pitot probes 93 times in 39 months, and the first mud in a probe is enough to upset the airspeed reading.

With the front opening and the drain hole both blocked, the pressure in the tube is trapped and, with the static port clear, the airspeed indicator works like an altimeter: it reads higher in a climb and lower in a descent, whatever the real speed.
Computed in the standard atmosphere, a tube sealed at 70 KIAS at 3,000 ft reads about 158 KIAS after a 1,000 ft climb with no change in real speed; 158 KIAS is the 172P's red line.
posts.intent: Your airspeed needle is only as honest as a tube under the left wing and a small hole in the side of the fuselage.

figure_key.points_at: The 172P's red line at 158 knots; the dial's printed red mark is ringed in white.

figure_key.label: 70 KT
figure_key.points_at: The airplane's real speed, 70 KIAS, unchanged through the climb, drawn as a glowing cyan outline needle that no real instrument has. The climb in cloud is shortened in time and the picture is not to scale.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: The airspeed indicator compares two pressures. Air rammed into the pitot tube under the left wing fills a diaphragm, and outside air from a static port fills the case around it. The needle shows the difference between them.

Block the tube's front with its drain hole clear and the needle falls to zero. Block the drain too and the needle follows altitude. Sealed at 70 KIAS (knots indicated airspeed), a 1,000 ft climb reads about 158, the 172P's red line.

article.heading: How the needle reads two pressures
paragraphs: On the Cessna 172P, the pitot tube hangs under the left wing. A pitot tube has a front opening and a small drain hole for moisture. The static port is a small hole low on the left side of the forward fuselage.
The front opening catches ram air at total pressure, the outside air's static pressure plus dynamic pressure, the extra pressure from motion.

A line carries it into a thin diaphragm inside the airspeed indicator. The case around it holds static pressure from the port, so the static part cancels and only dynamic pressure pushes. Fly faster and it grows. The diaphragm swells, and a linkage turns the needle.

figure.caption: Inside the airspeed indicator. Ram air (gold) fills the diaphragm, static air (light blue) fills the case around it, and the needle shows the difference. The cutaway follows the FAA handbook's generic airspeed indicator, not a Cessna parts drawing.
figure.alt: A cutaway of an airspeed indicator: a gold line labelled Ram air feeds a gold diaphragm inside a case filled light blue and labelled Static air, a linkage runs to the needle on the 172P's dial, and a banner above reads RAM minus STATIC to AIRSPEED.

article.heading: A blocked front reads zero
paragraphs: Ice, dirt or insects can block a pitot tube. A nest in the front can leave the drain hole as the only opening. The air inside vents through the drain to outside pressure. Both sides of the diaphragm match, so the needle reads zero.

At Brisbane Airport, 3D-printed replica probes, not the airplanes' real ones, were watched for 39 months. Mud-nesting keyhole wasps fully blocked them 93 times, the first within two weeks. Even the first mud upsets the airspeed reading.

figure.caption: An X-ray of the tube's front. The mud nest (red) stops the ram air (gold arrows), and the needle rests at zero. The drain hole (the light-blue disc) is drawn larger so it shows. Not to scale.
figure.alt: An X-ray of the pitot tube's cone in gold with a red mud plug labelled Mud nest in its front opening, gold arrows of ram air stopped at the plug, light-blue outside air inside the tube, a glowing light-blue drain hole underneath and an airspeed indicator inset at zero.

article.heading: Ice on both holes makes an altimeter
paragraphs: In visible moisture, ice can seal the drain hole as well as the front. The air in the tube is then trapped, and speed changes no longer reach the needle.
Now climb. The static pressure in the case falls while the trapped pressure stays, so the diaphragm swells and the needle rises. Descend and it falls. It now works like an altimeter.
In the standard atmosphere, a 1,000 ft climb from 3,000 ft lowers the case pressure by about an inch of mercury. The trapped pressure stays put, and the diaphragm reads that extra inch as speed.

That 158 assumes a perfect seal and trapped air that keeps its temperature. Sealed at sea level, the same climb reads about 164, and from 6,000 ft about 152. Let the trapped air cool by 1 °C and it reads about 152.

The 172P POH's inadvertent icing checklist starts with pitot heat on (if installed), then turn back or change altitude. Heat keeps the tube working in possible icing conditions, but the POH prohibits flight into icing conditions.

figure.caption: Rime ice building over the tube's front opening in cloud. Pitot heat, where installed, is there to keep the tube working in possible icing conditions, and the POH prohibits flight into icing conditions. Not to scale.
figure.alt: A close view from below of the pitot tube's cone in grey cloud, with white rime ice built up over its front opening and a red label Ice pointing at it.

article.heading: Three mistakes a blocked tube punishes
paragraphs: Remove the pitot tube cover and check the tube's front opening and drain hole on every preflight. A cover keeps bugs out of a parked airplane's tube.

Check the static source opening too. A blocked static port makes the airspeed read low above the altitude where it blocked, and high below it. The altimeter freezes and the vertical speed indicator reads zero. Some 172Ps have an alternate static source valve below the throttle, and POH Section 5 gives its effect on airspeed.

Watch the airspeed rise as the takeoff roll begins. At rest, a blocked tube reads zero too. A needle still at zero on the roll is abnormal, and the Airplane Flying Handbook says abnormal situations can require rejecting the takeoff while still on the runway.

figure.caption: The pitot tube is the small tube under the left wing, ringed and magnified here. The pictures on this page are frames of the reel, not to scale. Reel credits: 3D model “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified. Engine sound “1978 Cessna 172 Departure” by Wingspan Adventures & Flight (youtube.com), CC BY 3.0, modified.
figure.alt: A white Cessna 172P on the ramp, labelled CESSNA 172P, with the pitot tube under its left wing ringed in gold and labelled Pitot tube, and a magnified circle showing the tube.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. The airspeed stays at zero as your takeoff roll begins, so which blockage fits?
2. Sealed at 70 KIAS at 3,000 ft, what does the needle read after a 1,000 ft climb at the same speed?
3. You add power in level flight and the needle holds a normal-looking speed without moving, so which blockage fits?
4. Which openings do you check on the preflight so the airspeed indicator works?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. The tube's front opening, whether or not its drain hole is clear, because no ram air reaches the diaphragm.
2. About 158 KIAS, the red line, because the case pressure falls while the trapped pressure stays.
3. Both of the tube's openings. Trapped pressure ignores speed, and level flight holds the altitude too.
4. The tube's front opening and drain hole, with the cover off, and the static source opening.

posts.title: How the stall horn works
posts.headline: A slot in the left wing, a tube and a reed horn that runs on air.
posts.alt: An X-ray view of a white Cessna 172 with the stall warning tube, drawn in gold, running from the cabin along the left wing to the slot in its leading edge, where red arrows labelled AIR OUT leave it. Not to scale.
teaches: The Cessna 172P's stall warning is pneumatic, with an inlet in the leading edge of the left wing, an air-operated horn near the upper left corner of the windshield, and the plumbing between them.
At a low angle of attack the airflow virtually stops at a stagnation point close to the leading edge, where the stall warning inlet sits.

As the airplane approaches a stall, the point where the air splits moves under the leading edge, the low pressure on the upper surface moves forward around the leading edge, and the differential pressure draws air through the warning horn.

The horn sounds 5 to 10 knots above the stall in all flight conditions; it doesn't read airspeed, and stall warning devices alert the pilot when approaching the critical angle of attack, the angle at which a wing stalls regardless of airspeed.

Power off at 2,400 lb with flaps up, the 172P stalls at about 44 KIAS wings level and about 62 KIAS in a level 60-degree bank (POH Figure 5-3, approximate values); in that bank the load factor is 2, and the stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor.
On the preflight, check the stall warning opening for stoppage, then place a clean handkerchief over the opening and apply suction; a sound from the warning horn confirms the system works.
posts.intent: The Cessna 172P warns you of a stall with no wire and no switch.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 4
Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 5

figure_key.label: AIR OUT
figure_key.points_at: Air leaving the slot in the left wing, pulled from the cabin through the horn (the bell at the upper left) and along the tube, shown in gold with red pulses.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: The 172P's stall horn is pneumatic, and air drawn through it makes the sound. It reacts to angle of attack, the angle at which the wing meets the oncoming air, and it doesn't measure airspeed.
That is why it sounds 5 to 10 knots above the stall in all flight conditions, steep turns included. Test it on every walkaround with suction through a clean handkerchief over its opening.

article.heading: Where the inlet and the horn sit
paragraphs: Walk to the left wing and look at its leading edge, the rounded front edge that meets the air first. The small opening there is the stall warning inlet.
Plumbing runs from that inlet to an air-operated horn near the upper left corner of the windshield. The wing end senses the stall coming, and the horn makes the sound.

figure.caption: The stall warning inlet is the small slot in the left wing's leading edge, seen in the circle. The pictures on this page are frames of the reel, not to scale. 3D model: “Cessna172” by KOG_THORNS (sketchfab.com), CC BY 4.0, modified.
figure.alt: A white Cessna 172P seen from above over farmland, labelled CESSNA 172P and LEFT WING ONLY, with a magnified circle on the left wing's leading edge showing the dark inlet slot.

article.heading: What the air does at the inlet
paragraphs: At a low angle of attack the air meets the wing at a stagnation point. That is a spot close to the leading edge where the flow virtually stops. The inlet sits there, so the air just pushes in and the horn stays quiet.

Raise the nose and slow down. As the angle grows, the point where the air splits slides lower, under the leading edge. The low pressure on the upper surface moves forward around the leading edge, over the inlet.
The inlet now sits in lower pressure than the cabin air at the horn. That difference pulls cabin air in through the horn, along the tube and out of the slot. The reed sounds.

figure.caption: Nose up, the air now splits at the white dot, under the leading edge, and the blue dashes mark where it split at the slot in normal flight. The low pressure on top wraps forward over the gold slot. Not to scale.
figure.alt: A cross-section of the wing's leading edge at a high angle of attack, with dashed airflow lines curving around it and a red band labelled LOW PRESSURE wrapping forward over the gold slot.

article.heading: Why it still warns in a steep turn
paragraphs: For a given flap setting the 172P always stalls at the same angle of attack. Weight and bank angle don't change that angle.

The stall speed does change. Roll into a level 60-degree bank and the load factor, the load on the wing compared with straight-and-level flight, becomes 2. To hold altitude you add angle of attack, so the wing reaches its stall angle at a higher speed.

A load factor of 2 multiplies the stall speed by the square root of 2, about 1.41, a 41 percent rise. At 2,400 lb with flaps up and power off, that takes the stall from about 44 KIAS, knots of indicated airspeed, to about 62 KIAS.
The horn doesn't read airspeed. It answers the low pressure at the inlet, which follows the angle.

table.caption: Cessna 172P power-off stall speeds in KIAS (POH Figure 5-3) at 2,400 lb and the most rearward center of gravity, approximate as the POH gives them. At the most forward center of gravity the flaps 10° speeds are 2 to 3 knots higher.

article.heading: Three mistakes the horn invites
paragraphs: Check the stall warning opening for stoppage on every walkaround. It is item 3 of the left wing's leading edge check. Put a clean handkerchief over it before you apply suction, and a sound from the horn confirms the system works.

Ease the nose down when the horn sounds while you maneuver, whatever the airspeed indicator shows. In a steep turn it can sound at a speed that would feel comfortable wings level. Less angle of attack silences it. Then roll the wings level and add power. The POH notes that a stall recovery may lose as much as 230 feet.
Keep reading the wing's own cues when the horn stays quiet. A stall warning system can fail. Aerodynamic buffet, loss of roll authority or a descent you cannot stop still point to a stall.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. In a 172P at 2,400 lb, flaps up and power off, roughly what is the stall speed in a level 60-degree bank?
2. Why does a horn that doesn't read airspeed still sound before the stall in that steep turn?
3. You apply suction through a handkerchief over the stall warning opening and hear nothing, so what has the check told you?
4. Which cue do you trust when the airframe buffets and the ailerons lose authority but the horn stays quiet?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. About 62 KIAS. A load factor of 2 multiplies the 44 KIAS wings-level stall by the square root of 2, about 1.41. The horn sounds 5 to 10 knots above that.
2. It reacts to the low pressure reaching the inlet, which follows angle of attack. The wing stalls at the same angle in the turn, only at a higher speed.
3. Nothing proves it works yet. Check the opening for stoppage, seal the handkerchief and try again. If it stays silent, the stall warning isn't working, so have it fixed before you fly.
4. Trust the buffet and the weak ailerons. A stall warning system can fail, and those cues still tell you a stall is close, so lower the angle of attack.

posts.title: Compass acceleration error
posts.headline: Speed up heading east and the compass shows a turn toward north.
posts.alt: Compass acceleration error: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Speed up heading east and the compass shows a turn toward north.
teaches: On an easterly or westerly heading, accelerating makes the magnetic compass indicate a turn toward north, and decelerating a turn toward south; the memory aid is ANDS, Acceleration North, Deceleration South.
The error comes from the magnetic dip and the inertia of the pendulous card: accelerating tips the aft end of the card up and decelerating tips it down, and the dip acts on the tilted card.
On a north or south heading, diving, climbing or changing airspeed causes no compass error.

The compass indicates correctly only while its card is horizontal, so the swing during a speed change on an east or west heading is an error, not a turn; read the compass again once the speed is steady.
This is the Northern Hemisphere behaviour, where Earth's magnetic field dips down into the ground, more steeply nearer the Magnetic North Pole.
posts.intent: A change of speed on an east or west heading makes the magnetic compass show a turn that isn't happening. Here is why, and what to do about it.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 8

figure_key.label: Speeding up
figure_key.points_at: The aircraft flying east along the road, gaining speed with its wings level.

figure_key.label: Shows north
figure_key.points_at: The compass, whose card has swung toward north although the nose has not moved.

figure_key.label: Compass
figure_key.points_at: The yellow arrow showing where the compass says the nose points, left of the road toward north.

figure_key.label: N
figure_key.points_at: The arrow showing north.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: On an east or west heading, the compass shows a turn toward north as you gain speed and toward south as you lose it. Pilots carry it as ANDS, Acceleration North, Deceleration South.
That swing is an error, so keep the wings level and take a fresh reading once the airspeed stops changing.

article.heading: How the compass card hangs
paragraphs: Inside the compass, two small magnets ride on a metal float, sealed in a bowl of clear fluid much like kerosene. The card is a scale wrapped around the float. You read it through a window against the lubber line, a fixed mark across the glass.
Its letters mark north, east, south and west, with a number every 30° between them and the last zero left off. So 3 means 30°, 6 means 60° and 33 means 330°.

The float hangs from a pivot with its centre of gravity below it, like a pendulum. Earth's magnetic field runs level with the ground only at the Magnetic Equator, halfway between the magnetic poles. Everywhere else it tilts, and that tilt against the ground is called magnetic dip.

Because the float hangs low and is heavy, the field's downward pull is too weak to tip it, so the card stays level. This hanging, or pendulous, mounting is what lets one compass work at all latitudes away from the poles without a correction for dip.

article.heading: Why a speed change tips the card
paragraphs: Picture yourself eastbound, pushing the power up. The float has inertia, the tendency of a mass to resist a change in its motion, so it lags behind as the airplane gathers speed. That lag tips the aft end of the card up, so its front tips down. Slowing down tips it the other way.

Now the card is no longer level, and the compass reads correctly only while it is. On the tilted card, the field's downward pull drags the magnet's north end down, and that turns the card so the reading swings toward north.
That rotation of the card is acceleration error. The reading moves although your heading hasn't, and it stops once a steady speed lets the card hang level again.
Everything here is the Northern Hemisphere case. There the field dips downward toward the north, and the dip grows steeper as you near the Magnetic North Pole.

figure.caption: Speeding up eastbound, the card's front tips down, and the dip pulls it so the reading swings toward north.
figure.alt: A high-wing trainer seen from the side over farmland, below a compass card drawn as a tilted dark disc with labels Front down and Magnetic dip, magenta arrows sloping into the ground, Northern Hemisphere above, and a compass reading between E and 6 labelled Speeding up and Shows north.

article.heading: Which headings show the error
paragraphs: Point the nose north or south and a speed change brings no compass error. Climbing and diving on those headings bring none either.
East and west are where it shows. Eastbound, a false turn toward north makes the heading numbers fall, and westbound it makes them rise. Slowing down reverses both.

figure.caption: Heading north, the same speed change leaves the compass on N.
figure.alt: A trainer seen from above flying north along a road, labelled Speeding up, beside a compass reading N with the label No swing.

article.heading: Three easy mistakes with a power change
paragraphs: Hold the wings level and let the card swing. Turning to chase the reading back steers you off a heading you never left.

Set the heading indicator, the gyro instrument you line up with the compass, only in steady flight. Set it during a speed change and it copies the error. If the card still wobbles once you're steady, use the average of its swings.

Make power changes smoothly and read the compass only once the airspeed has settled, not when the throttle stops moving. Abrupt changes of speed or attitude send the card moving erratically and make it very hard to read.

figure.caption: Hold the wings level through the swing: the red airplane chased it and ended off its heading.
figure.alt: A trainer seen from above flying west along a road with the label Speed steady and a compass reading W, and a red airplane turned off the road below it, labelled Off heading, with its own compass.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. What has your heading done if, flying east, the reading creeps from E toward 6 while the speed builds after you add power?
2. Are you turning if, heading west with the wings level, the reading slides from W toward 24 as you slow down?
3. Should the compass swing when you're flying north and the airspeed rises after you add power?
4. Should you set the heading indicator to the compass while flying east with the speed still building?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. It hasn't changed. That swing is acceleration error, and 6 means 60°, on the north side of E.
2. No. 24 sits on the south side of W, which is exactly where slowing down drags the reading on a west heading.
3. No. North is one of the two headings where a change of airspeed brings no compass error.
4. No. Wait until the speed is steady, or you set the heading indicator to the false turn toward north.

posts.title: Magnetic compass errors
posts.headline: Turning toward north, roll out before the compass shows north.
posts.alt: Magnetic compass errors: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Turning toward north, roll out before the compass shows north.
teaches: The magnetic compass reads correctly only while its card is horizontal; in a bank the card tilts with the airplane, and the dip of Earth's magnetic field then turns it.

In the Northern Hemisphere, turning toward north the reading falls behind the real heading (the handbooks say the card leads), so stop the turn before the compass reaches north; turning toward south the reading runs ahead (the card lags), so let the compass pass south first.
One rule of thumb is 15 degrees plus half the latitude, early toward north and late toward south: near 40 degrees north that is 15 + 20 = 35 degrees.
On an easterly or westerly heading, accelerating shows a turn toward north and decelerating a turn toward south (ANDS); on a north or south heading, a change of airspeed causes no error.

The float and card tilt freely to about 18 degrees of bank, and the compass reads erratically in a steeper bank; after a roll-out the card swings around the heading before it settles, so use the average of the swings.
posts.intent: Steering by the magnetic compass alone, its reading is only right while the card is level. Near north it falls behind a turn and near south it runs ahead, so you stop early toward north and late toward south.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 8

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Steering by the magnetic compass in the Northern Hemisphere, stop a turn to north before the compass reaches north. On a turn to south, let the compass pass south before you stop. Near 40 degrees north, one rule of thumb makes each allowance about 35 degrees.

article.heading: Why the card reads wrong in a bank
paragraphs: Magnets on a float line it up with Earth's field. A card on the float carries the headings, read at the lubber line.
Earth's magnetic field runs level with the ground only at the magnetic equator. Nearer the magnetic north pole it slopes down into the ground, and that angle is called dip.

The float sits on a pivot and is weighted below it, so it hangs like a pendulum, too heavy for dip to tip. In a coordinated bank it hangs toward the airplane's own floor, so the card tilts with the airplane, and dip starts to turn it.

Turning toward north, dip swings the tilted card the same way you turn, so the lubber line's number falls behind your real heading. Turning toward south, the card is held back and the number runs ahead. The handbooks say it from the card's side: the card leads toward north and lags toward south.

figure.caption: Banked left toward north, the card tilts with the airplane and dip drags it the same way you turn, so its reading falls behind.
figure.alt: Seen from behind, a high-wing trainer banks left over farmland below a tilted compass card drawn as a dark disc. Magenta arrows show Earth's field dipping into the ground, and labels read Northern Hemisphere, Magnetic dip, Tilted card, and 035 Falls behind.

article.heading: Sizing the roll-out for your latitude
paragraphs: The error grows nearer the magnetic poles, so the allowance depends on latitude. The FAA's Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge offers one rule of thumb: 15 degrees plus half your latitude.

The Instrument Flying Handbook gives a second method for compass turns at a 15 to 18 degree bank. Turning to north, start the roll-out about your latitude before north, plus the few degrees you normally allow for rolling out. Turning to south, start it once the compass has passed south by about your latitude, minus those few degrees. Its example, from east at 30 degrees north in a 15 degree bank, starts the roll-out at 037 for north and 203 for south.
The two give different numbers because both are rough. Whichever you use, roll out, let the card settle, then correct with small turns.

With the first rule, flying east near 40 degrees north, that is 15 + 20 = 35 degrees. Turning left to north, stop the turn when the compass reads 035, and the card settles on north. Turning right to south, let it pass south and stop the turn at 215.

figure.caption: Near 40 degrees north the rule of thumb gives 35 degrees both ways: stop the turn at 035 turning from east to north, and at 215 turning from east to south.
figure.alt: Two trainers seen from above, side by side. Under East to N, a compass reads 035 and the label says Early: 035. Under East to S, a compass reads 215 and the label says Late: 215. Below them: Undershoot N, overshoot S.

article.heading: False turns on the compass
paragraphs: Start a turn from a northerly heading and the reading at first falls behind, and may even show a turn the other way. Start one from a southerly heading and the reading runs ahead, showing more turn than you have made.
On an east or west heading, speed up and the compass swings toward north with your wings level. Slow down and it swings south. The memory aid is ANDS, Acceleration North, Deceleration South.
On a north or south heading, changing speed, climbing or diving causes no error.

article.heading: Three mistakes on a compass turn
paragraphs: Keep the bank under about 18 degrees in a compass turn. The float and card tilt freely only to about that angle, and in a steeper bank the readings turn erratic.
Read the average of the swings after you roll out, because the card swings around your heading before it settles.
Change attitude and airspeed smoothly, because abrupt changes set the card swinging erratically and make it very hard to read.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. Flying east near 40 degrees north, you turn left toward north, so at what compass reading do you stop the turn?
2. Using 15 plus half the latitude near 30 degrees north, how far past south should the compass go before you stop the turn?
3. On a steady westerly heading, the compass swings toward north as you speed up, so should you bank to correct it?
4. Flying north, you roll into a right turn and the compass briefly shows a turn to the left, so is the compass faulty?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. At about 035, because 15 plus half of 40 is 35, and the card then settles on north.
2. By 30 degrees, because half of 30 is 15, and 15 plus 15 is 30.
3. No, keep the wings level. That swing is acceleration error, the A in ANDS, not a turn.
4. No. Starting a turn from a northerly heading, the reading falls behind at first and can briefly show a turn the other way.

posts.title: A microburst on final
posts.headline: Your headwind on entry becomes a tailwind on exit.
posts.alt: Cover slide titled Microbursts. A storm cell drops a heavy rain shaft beyond an airfield at dusk, with a Cessna 172 on final and the control tower at right. Text: Fly through one and a 45-knot headwind can become a 45-knot tailwind, a few hundred feet up.
caption: Fly through a microburst and a 45-knot headwind can become a 45-knot tailwind, a few hundred feet above the ground. Here's how to spot one, why a sudden airspeed jump is a warning, and why you can't count on getting one.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: A microburst produces a headwind gain on entry followed by a downdraft and then a tailwind on exit.
The initial airspeed increase is the warning, and reducing power to correct it removes the margin needed moments later.
posts.intent: The same microburst gives a performance-increasing headwind first and a performance-losing tailwind second.

figure_key.label: HEADWIND ON ENTRY, AIRSPEED UP
figure_key.points_at: The ghost aircraft's nose, where the left-running outflow meets it head-on.

figure_key.label: DO NOT REDUCE POWER
figure_key.points_at: The crest of the dotted flight-path trace, where it bulges highest above the glidepath.

figure_key.label: TAILWIND ON EXIT, AIRSPEED FALLING
figure_key.points_at: The solid aircraft's tail, where the right-running outflow overtakes it.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A microburst on final gives you a headwind that raises your airspeed, then a downdraft, then a tailwind that takes it away. That early gain is the warning. Don't reduce power to fix it, and be ready to go around. The margin you would trim off is the margin you need moments later.

article.heading: What a microburst does to the wind
paragraphs: Picture a column of air dropping out of a shower or thunderstorm and spreading outward in all directions when it reaches the ground. That is a microburst, the most severe kind of wind shear, meaning a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a small area.
Going in, the outflow, the air racing away from the center, meets you as a headwind. In the middle the air pushes you down, and coming out the outflow runs your way as a tailwind.

Vertical winds usually peak more than 500 ft above the ground. In the center of a strong microburst, the downdraft can exceed 3,000 fpm (feet per minute). How hard it hits you depends on your height and how near the center you pass.

table.caption: The size and strength of a typical microburst.

figure.caption: A microburst: a small, intense downdraft falls from the cloud and spreads out along the ground in every direction.
figure.alt: A dense rain column falls from a dark storm cloud onto farmland near an airfield and spreads outward at the ground. A blue arrow down the column is labelled downdraft, and arrows along the ground each way are labelled outflow.

article.heading: Why the airspeed gain is a trap
paragraphs: A rising headwind lifts your indicated airspeed and performance. The nose tends to pitch up as the airplane works back to its trim speed, leaving you fast and high.

Correcting that with less power and a lower nose sets up what comes next. The tailwind arrives and takes away airspeed and performance, and it finds you nose low with the power back. Recovery from there is harder, and the airplane can stall or land short of the runway.
So treat a rapid or large airspeed gain near convective weather, meaning showers and storms, as a possible sign of a coming loss. It may be reason enough to break off the approach.

figure.caption: The headwind's airspeed gain tempts you to take off power and lower the nose, so when the tailwind takes that airspeed away you sink below the approach path and land short of the runway.
figure.alt: The headwind's airspeed gain tempts you to take off power and lower the nose, so when the tailwind takes that airspeed away you sink below the approach path and land short of the runway.

article.heading: When the warning never comes
paragraphs: A microburst's outflow can be symmetric, the same on every side, but it is often asymmetric, stronger on some sides than others. Depending on your path, the gain going in may never appear, or may be much smaller than the loss coming out.

An intense rain shaft at the surface can mark a microburst. Sometimes the only visible clue is virga, rain streaks that never reach the ground, or a ring of blowing dust. If you've met or seen one, watch for another, since the same weather system can produce more than one.

figure.caption: Virga and a ring of blowing dust can be the only signs a microburst gives.
figure.alt: Grey streaks of virga hang from a dark cloud base over an airfield, fading before they reach the ground, and a ring of blowing dust spreads along the fields below. Both are labelled.

article.heading: Three easy mistakes in a microburst
paragraphs: Go around at the first sign of a microburst. Only 5 to 15 seconds may be available to recognize it and recover. At low altitude, recovery may be impossible.

Hold the nose at its normal pitch or higher as the airspeed falls, and accept the slower speed. The airplane's natural response to low airspeed is to pitch down, and letting it go there adds to the height you lose.
Fly a stabilized approach, holding one steady speed and path, so a bad trend stands out early. Feeding in power bit by bit may mask the first drop in airspeed.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. What should a sudden jump well above your target airspeed on final near a shower tell you?
2. Can you rule out a microburst near the airport if you see virga below the cloud base but no rain at the surface?
3. How should you handle pitch when the airspeed starts falling partway down final and the nose wants to drop?
4. If you fly into a microburst's outflow and feel no airspeed gain at all, can you expect a gentle exit?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. It may be a microburst's headwind, with a tailwind loss to follow. Keep the power in and be ready to go around.
2. No. Virga or a ring of blowing dust is sometimes the only visible sign of a microburst.
3. Hold pitch at normal or higher and accept the lower airspeed. Letting the nose drop to chase speed costs height you can't spare.
4. No. In an asymmetric microburst the gain going in may be small or missing, and the loss coming out much larger.

posts.title: Going around: power first
posts.headline: The moment you go around, power comes first.
posts.alt: Going around: power first: an illustrated diagram for pilots. The moment you go around, power comes first. The picture shows the house aircraft right of centre, nose raised a few degrees, climbing away from the runway; a ghost of the house aircraft below and slightly behind it, nose level, still descending toward the touchdown zone; two thin pale flight paths that part above the threshold, one bending up to the solid aircraft and one continuing down to the ghost; a blurred propeller disc on the solid aircraft. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Why does power come before attitude and configuration in a go-around?

Power goes in the instant you decide to go around, full and smooth, with no hesitation. Expect two reactions. The added power raises the nose and yaws the airplane left, so forward pressure and right rudder hold a safe attitude.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: A go-around rests on three cardinal principles: power, attitude and configuration.
Power is the first concern: the instant you decide to go around, apply full power smoothly and without hesitation.
The added power raises the nose and yaws the airplane left, so expect forward pressure and right rudder to hold a safe attitude.
posts.intent: In a go-around power comes first, because it is what stops the sink; attitude and configuration follow.

figure_key.label: FULL POWER, NO HESITATION
figure_key.points_at: The propeller disc of the solid house aircraft.

figure_key.label: NOSE RISES, YAWS LEFT
figure_key.points_at: The nose and spinner of the solid house aircraft.

figure_key.label: FORWARD PRESSURE, RIGHT RUDDER
figure_key.points_at: The tail of the solid house aircraft, where the rudder and elevator meet.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A go-around, abandoning a landing to climb away, rests on three principles, which are power, attitude and configuration. The instant you decide, push in full power smoothly and without hesitation, and hold it until flying speed and control are back.

As the nose tries to rise and swing left, hold a safe attitude, its position against the horizon, with forward pressure and right rudder. The configuration, here the flaps, changes last, once the descent has stopped.

article.heading: Why the throttle moves before the yoke
paragraphs: A sinking airplane has inertia, a tendency to keep moving the way it already is, and it takes enough power to overcome it. Pitching up alone raises the angle of attack, the angle at which the wing meets the oncoming air, and bleeds off airspeed. The result is a faster sink, a stall close to the ground, or both.

Below stall speed an airplane cannot fly, and below minimum power required speed, where level flight takes the least power, it cannot climb. So resist pitching up for the climb until the airspeed is there, and in some cases lower the nose briefly to gain speed.

Full power here means full or maximum allowable takeoff power, put in positively. In some airplanes a jab at the throttle makes the engine falter, so keep the push smooth. If yours has carburetor heat, turn it off for maximum power.

article.heading: Holding the nose once the power is in
paragraphs: Expect to push hard to hold the nose level or in a safe climb attitude. Your trim, which takes the load off the controls, is still set for the slow approach. If the nose rises too early in a low go-around, the stall that follows could be unrecoverable.
The swing to the left comes from torque and P-factor, the left-turning effects of the engine and propeller under full power. Use as much right rudder as it takes to cancel them.
Once the speed is right and the climb pitch is set, give it a rough trim, a quick setting that eases the pressure. Fine-tune the trim when things have settled.

article.heading: Bringing the flaps up without losing lift
paragraphs: Fly the airplane before you reach for the flap handle. In airplanes with heavy control pressures at maximum power, reach for it with caution, because control comes first.

Bring the landing flaps partway up first, or to the takeoff setting, as the manufacturer recommends. Depending on height and speed, it is wise to raise them in small steps, giving the airplane time to speed up. Pulling them all up at once could take away lift and settle the airplane onto the ground.

figure.caption: What each of the three principles asks of your hands and feet, from the decision until the flaps are up.
figure.alt: What each of the three principles asks of your hands and feet, from the decision until the flaps are up.

article.heading: Two mistakes that spoil a go-around
paragraphs: Go around the moment the landing looks uncertain. The maneuver is not dangerous in itself, only when it is delayed unduly or flown badly. Delay normally comes from expecting the landing to work out, or from pride that treats going around as failure.

Don't trust the cushion of air you feel just above the runway. Near the ground the wing makes less induced drag, the drag that comes with making lift, and that is ground effect. That help is borrowed and repaid as you climb out. Climb too soon and you may not be able to climb, or even hold altitude, at full power.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. You decide to go around over the threshold with the airplane sinking, so why does power go in before you pull back?
2. Low and slow with full power just in, you feel the nose climbing by itself, so how do you respond?
3. How should full flaps come up once the descent has stopped and your climb is set?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. It takes power to overcome the sinking airplane's inertia. Pulling back alone bleeds speed toward a faster sink, a low stall, or both.
2. Push firmly forward to hold the nose level or in a safe climb attitude, with right rudder to keep straight. Letting it rise early this low risks an unrecoverable stall.
3. Partway up or to the manufacturer's takeoff setting first, then in small steps as speed builds. All at once could cost lift and settle you onto the ground.

posts.title: What flight following does not do
posts.headline: With flight following on, the lookout is still yours.
posts.alt: What flight following does not do: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With flight following on, the lookout is still yours. The picture shows a small radar antenna on a far hilltop at the left edge with five or six thin pale lines fanning out to the right; the lowest radar line grazing the crest of a substantial ridge just right of centre; a lee valley on the ridge's right side in deep shadow, below the lowest radar line, with no line entering it; the solid house aircraft upper right of centre, nose right, wings level, inside the radar lines. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Does flight following mean ATC will call out every airplane near you?

Radar limits and a busy controller both cut the traffic calls you hear, as do heavy traffic and a crowded frequency. A quiet frequency is no proof of an empty sky. Seeing and avoiding other aircraft stays with you.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Radar traffic information can be limited by the radar itself, the volume of traffic, controller workload and frequency congestion.
The service does not relieve the pilot of the responsibility to see and avoid other aircraft.
posts.intent: Flight following is a second set of eyes that can blink, so the lookout is still yours.

figure_key.label: RADAR CAN'T SEE HERE
figure_key.points_at: The shadowed wedge of the lee valley on the ridge's right side, just below the lowest radar line.

figure_key.label: NO TRAFFIC CALL
figure_key.points_at: The ghost of the house aircraft climbing out of the shadowed lee valley.

figure_key.label: SEE AND AVOID, STILL YOURS
figure_key.points_at: The house aircraft's windscreen.

article.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Flight following is radar traffic advice that ATC gives a VFR pilot who asks for it. The controller tells you about targets close enough to your position or route to deserve a look. Some targets may never get a call, for reasons you can't see from the cockpit. Keep watching for other aircraft and keep clear of them yourself, all flight, because the service never takes that over.

article.heading: Why a traffic call may never come
paragraphs: Picture a long, quiet stretch on frequency while you cruise with flight following. Nothing may be near you, or a call may have had no way to reach you.

Many things could stop a call. Among them are the radar's own limits, the volume of traffic, the controller's workload and a crowded frequency. A controller tied up with other airplanes, or a frequency with no gap to speak in, can leave your call unsaid.
The controller alone decides whether they can give the service, or keep giving it. They needn't tell you the reason, so the quiet doesn't tell you which case you're in.

Some traffic may not show on the screen at all. If part of the radar is out of service, ATC normally says so. Then the display shows only aircraft reporting through a transponder or ADS-B, and anything without them in use can't be called.

article.heading: Why the clock position can be off
paragraphs: A call tells you where to look, on the 12-hour clock around your airplane. A typical one is traffic 10 o'clock, 3 miles, westbound, with distance in nautical miles. Type and altitude follow only if known.

The controller sees only your track, the path over the ground, and never your heading, where the nose points. When you crab, angling the nose into the wind to hold your track, the two differ. Your clock turns with the nose, but the call's clock stays lined up with the track.
In the AIM's example, traffic called at 12 o'clock would appear at 2 o'clock to one pilot and 10 o'clock to another. A call of 2 o'clock would appear at 3 o'clock to a third.
A fourth pilot, needing no wind correction, would see the traffic right where it was called, at 11 o'clock. Turning just as a call comes in can throw it off the same way.
Altitude has its own gap. Radar gives none unless the other airplane has Mode C, the transponder feature that reports altitude, and the facility can display it.

figure.caption: The call is set to your track, so with the nose crabbed left, traffic called at 12 o'clock sits at 2 o'clock through the windscreen.
figure.alt: The call is set to your track, so with the nose crabbed left, traffic called at 12 o'clock sits at 2 o'clock through the windscreen.

article.heading: Three mistakes with flight following
paragraphs: Keep scanning the whole sky after a call, well beyond the spot it named. A call covers one target the controller saw and had time to report, and others may be nearby with no call at all.
Treat a called altitude as a lead to confirm with your eyes. It may come from Mode C that nobody has checked against what that pilot reports.

Choose your own way to keep clear once you see the traffic. The service gives no vector, a heading to fly away from traffic, unless you ask for one. Even then, the controller gives it only as far as they can.

article.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: 1. On a busy frequency, flight following has gone a long stretch without a traffic call, so can you treat the sky as clear?
2. You're crabbing with the nose left of your track when ATC calls traffic at 12 o'clock, so where should you look first?
3. ATC calls traffic with an altitude taken from its Mode C, so can you count on that altitude being right?
4. Traffic the controller called is in sight and closing, so should you hold your heading until ATC turns you?

article.heading: Answers
paragraphs: 1. No. A busy frequency is one of the things that can stop calls, and the controller needn't tell you why, so keep scanning.
2. Look right of the nose. The call's clock is set to your track, and your track runs right of where the nose points.
3. No. It may be unverified, so find the traffic and judge its height yourself.
4. No. Act to keep clear yourself as soon as you need to, because ATC won't turn you away from traffic on its own.

posts.title: Where Class G ends
posts.headline: Rising ground can lift Class E's floor above you.
posts.alt: A forested ridge under a blue Class E floor that follows the ground, 1,200 ft AGL above the crest. A Cessna holding 3,500 feet MSL is 1,000 ft AGL over the crest, below the floor, in Class G. Printed above is the subtraction 3,500 minus 2,500 equals 1,000 ft. Not to scale.
teaches: Class G is the uncontrolled airspace not designated Class A, B, C, D or E, and it runs from the surface up to the base of the overlying Class E, which is 1,200 feet AGL unless the chart designates otherwise.

A floor set in feet AGL rises and falls with the terrain; over a 1,500-foot MSL valley a 1,200-foot AGL floor lies at 2,700 feet MSL, and over a 2,500-foot MSL crest at 3,700 feet MSL, so an airplane holding 3,500 feet MSL passes from Class E into Class G where no Class B, C or D is designated.

Under 14 CFR 91.155 an airplane in Class G at or below 1,200 feet above the surface needs 1 statute mile and clear of clouds by day; by night it needs 3 statute miles and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds, as in Class E below 10,000 feet MSL; at night in a traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway it may instead fly clear of clouds with at least 1 statute mile.

Class G more than 1,200 feet above the surface and below 10,000 feet MSL needs 1 statute mile by day and 3 statute miles by night, with 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds; under 14 CFR 91.155(e) an aircraft operating at the base altitude of a Class E area is considered to be within the airspace directly below it.

Near airports with an approved instrument procedure, Class E transition areas, for aircraft transitioning to and from the terminal or en route environment, often begin at 700 feet AGL, marked by a magenta vignette, and they remain in effect continuously, regardless of airport operating hours or surface area status.

A Class E surface area, drawn with a magenta dashed line, brings Class E down to the surface; a surface area operating less than continuously is indicated by a note on the sectional, the airport's Chart Supplement page gives its status, and a part-time surface area may become Class G while it is not in effect.

A blue vignette marks floors other than 700 feet that border Class G, a 700-foot floor keeps its magenta vignette where it borders Class G, differing floors above 700 feet carry a symbol and a number, and some Class E begins at an MSL altitude that stays level; except where Class E is designated lower, it begins at 14,500 feet MSL and extends up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL, so there Class G reaches up to 14,500 feet MSL; that Class E leaves out the air less than 1,500 feet above the surface.
posts.intent: Hold one altitude over rising ground and you can pass from Class E into Class G without touching the controls, because Class E's floor is measured from the ground.

FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide (VFR Terms and Symbols), page 17

figure_key.points_at: The airspace around the airplane, under the floor that rose with the ridge.

figure_key.label: 3,500 – 2,500 = 1,000 ft
