article.heading: Why ice needs cloud and cold together
paragraphs: Picture a climb out through a solid overcast with the ground falling away. You are wet the whole way up, but moisture alone does not make ice.

Structural icing, the ice that builds on the outside of the airframe, needs two things at the same time. One is visible moisture, such as cloud or rain. The other is an airframe surface at or below freezing.

For the air, the handbooks are plain about it. The outside air temperature, or OAT, has to be below 0 °C for icing to happen. There is one exception, covered further down, because the airframe does not always match the air.

Ice matters because of what it does to airflow, far more than its weight. Frost or ice no rougher than coarse sandpaper on the leading edge or top of the wing can cut lift by 30 percent. That same thin layer can raise drag by up to 40 percent, and bigger buildups by 80 percent or more.

article.heading: Where the freezing level hides in cloud
paragraphs: The freezing level is the height where the air temperature passes through 0 °C. Higher air is typically colder, which is why the handbooks list temperature and altitude together.
A cloud layer does not stop at the freezing level. One layer can straddle it, with its lower part in air above zero and its upper part in air below.
Climb through that layer and you cross the line while still inside the cloud. The moisture around you is the same before and after. Only the temperature changed, and the cloud gives no sign of it.
That makes the climb itself the decision. Below the line, the cloud supplies moisture and the air is above freezing. Above it, the cloud supplies both ingredients at once.

article.heading: How cold the icing band usually is
paragraphs: Passing 0 °C does not mean more ice with every degree. Clouds hold supercooled water, liquid drops colder than freezing, and the colder the cloud gets, the less of it there is. Eventually only ice crystals remain.
That is why icing bunches into a band of temperature and height. High stratiform cloud colder than -20 °C is mostly ice crystals and gives little icing. The table shows where the reports gather.

Temperature also shapes the kind of ice. Rime, the rough milky kind, tends to form colder than -15 °C, and mixed ice forms between that and -10 °C. Clear ice, glossy and hard to see, tends to form warmer than -10 °C.
So the first degrees past the freezing level are clear ice territory. The handbooks call this general guidance, since drop size, water content and the aircraft itself change the result.

table.caption: Where icing reports cluster, as FAA-H-8083-28 and AC 00-6B give them
rows: The only physical cold limit, where liquid drops freeze on their own

article.heading: When the airframe is colder than the air
paragraphs: Say you have been flying in cold air and then descend into air above 0 °C. The airframe does not warm up to the air temperature straight away.
This is called cold soaking. A cold-soaked airframe can stay below 0 °C for some time, and on some aircraft it stays that cold even after landing.
Aircraft with fuel tanks mounted flush to the skin are especially prone to this. They can pick up ice in air only slightly above 0 °C.
So an OAT reading just above zero is not a clean bill of health in cloud. How long an airframe holds the cold varies from type to type, so know your own aircraft's limits.

article.heading: Why the top of a layer ices most
paragraphs: Flat, layered cloud is called stratiform. In low and middle stratiform layers, icing on average sits in a band 3,000 to 4,000 ft thick, and it usually runs from trace to light.
The strongest icing in these layers is in the upper part of the cloud. In a climb where the freezing level sits mid-layer, that upper part is exactly where you arrive after crossing it.
The shallow band helps you. A change of only a few thousand feet may take you out of the icing, even while you stay in cloud. The catch is that these layers spread a very long way sideways.

Heaped cloud, called cumuliform, is built differently. Its icing is narrower but taller, and in a building cloud it runs through every level above the freezing level. It is worst near the top, where the updraft is concentrated.

article.heading: When descending does not get you out
paragraphs: Going down to warmer air has a trap near fronts, which is where most icing reports come from. Under a front, air above freezing can sit on top of a layer below freezing.
Rain forms up in the warm air and falls into the cold layer underneath. The drops cool below freezing but stay liquid, which makes them supercooled. They freeze the moment they strike an aircraft.

This is a favoured spot for severe clear icing, because there is so much supercooled water. If the cold layer is shallow, the rain reaches the ground as freezing rain. If it is deep, the drops freeze into ice pellets, and ice pellets mean icing above.
Freezing rain often covers a broad area. With the cold air underneath you, a pilot may be unable to escape it by descending.

figure.caption: Rain made in the warm air above the front turns supercooled in the cold wedge below it, and that wedge is where the aircraft is.
figure.alt: Rain made in the warm air above the front turns supercooled in the cold wedge below it, and that wedge is where the aircraft is.

article.heading: What to do when ice starts
paragraphs: Whatever ice protection your aircraft has, the first move is to leave the visible moisture. That could mean descending below the cloud bases, climbing above the tops, or turning onto a different course.
If none of those is possible, move to an altitude where the temperature is above freezing. Under freezing rain that may not work, and near mountains the terrain may stop you from descending to it.
Ice also feeds itself once it starts. Adding power and raising the nose to hold altitude increases the angle of attack, and that lets ice collect on the underside of the wings and fuselage.

posts.title: Carburettor ice on a warm day
posts.headline: Your carburettor makes its own cold, whatever the OAT.
posts.alt: Carburettor ice on a warm day: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your carburettor makes its own cold, whatever the OAT. The picture shows a rendered single-engine aeroplane in level cruise, small and high in the frame, over hazy summer farmland; a large cutaway of its carburettor filling the near foreground, sectioned along the induction path so intake mouth, venturi throat and throttle plate all read; pale streamlines entering the intake mouth and squeezing through the narrow throat, with the fuel spray leaving the nozzle in that same throat; a granular rime collar around the partly closed throttle plate, feathering thinner up the bore wall behind it. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: How does carburettor ice form when the outside air is well above freezing?

Fuel vaporising in the venturi absorbs heat, and the pressure drop through it cools the induction air further. The charge can end up below freezing. A warm OAT is what makes the risk easy to dismiss, and reduced power in humid air is when it shows up.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Fuel vaporisation and the pressure drop through the venturi cool the induction air substantially below ambient.
Carburettor ice is therefore possible at outside air temperatures well above freezing, particularly at high humidity and reduced power.
posts.intent: The temperature drop happens inside the carburettor, so ice forms on a day well above freezing.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 7

figure_key.label: WARM, HUMID AIR HERE
figure_key.points_at: The flared intake mouth of the cutaway, where outside air enters.

figure_key.label: COLDER THAN OUTSIDE AIR
figure_key.points_at: The narrow venturi throat, at the point the fuel spray leaves the nozzle.

figure_key.label: ICE NARROWING THE GAP
figure_key.points_at: The rime collar on the partly closed throttle plate and the shrunken air gap past it.

figure_key.label: PLATE OPEN, BORE CLEAR
figure_key.points_at: The ghost cutaway's wide-open throttle plate and clean bore.

article.heading: Where the cold comes from
paragraphs: Start with a warm, humid day and a float-type carburettor, the more common type and the one small aircraft usually carry. It is named for a float that rests on the fuel in its float chamber, the bowl that feeds the carburettor. Outside air passes through a filter, usually at the front of the cowling, and enters through the air inlet.

Inside, the air passes through the venturi, a narrow throat in the carburettor. The venturi's shape creates an area of low pressure. Fuel in the float chamber sits at higher pressure, so it is pushed out of the discharge nozzle into that throat.

Two things now cool the air. Its pressure has dropped, and the fuel is turning from liquid to vapour, which is called vaporisation. Together they make a sharp temperature drop right inside the carburettor.

The discharge nozzle must sit at the venturi throat, where the pressure is low. The throttle valve, worked by the throttle in the cockpit, sits on the engine side of the nozzle. So the fuel cools the air inside the venturi, and ice forms readily there and on the throttle valve.

A pressure-type carburettor, rarely found on small aircraft, sprays fuel under pressure on the engine side of the throttle valve. There, engine heat offsets the cooling, and the risk of fuel vaporisation icing almost disappears.

figure.caption: Fuel enters at the venturi throat, ahead of the throttle valve, which is why ice collects in both places.
figure.alt: Fuel enters at the venturi throat, ahead of the throttle valve, which is why ice collects in both places.

article.heading: How much colder the carburettor gets
paragraphs: The FAA's Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25, chapter 7) puts the temperature drop at as much as 60 to 70 Fahrenheit degrees. Read that as a difference on the scale, not a temperature of 70 °F.
Converting a difference takes care. Water freezes and boils 180 degrees apart in Fahrenheit and 100 degrees apart in Celsius. So a drop of 70 Fahrenheit degrees is 38.89 Celsius degrees.

Now run the handbook's own example. Air at 100 °F (38 °C) that loses 70 Fahrenheit degrees is at 30 °F (-1 °C) inside the carburettor. That carburettor air is below freezing, 32 °F (0 °C), on a day you would call hot.
The FAA's weather handbook, AC 00-6B, gives a similar figure. It says carburetion, the mixing of fuel and air, can cool the incoming air by as much as 33 °C.

figure.caption: On the handbook's 100 °F day, a 70-degree drop leaves the carburettor air below the freezing line.
figure.alt: On the handbook's 100 °F day, a 70-degree drop leaves the carburettor air below the freezing line.

article.heading: Why a warm day is no protection
paragraphs: Cold air on its own makes no ice. Water vapour, the water carried invisibly in the air, has to condense into liquid while the carburettor is at or below freezing. When it does, ice may form on the surfaces inside, the throttle valve among them.
So the day's moisture matters too. Relative humidity tells you how close the air is to saturation, the point where it can hold no more water vapour. At 100 percent the air is saturated.

The Pilot's Handbook rates ice most likely below 70 °F (21 °C) with relative humidity above 80 percent. Because the cooling is so sharp, it also says icing can happen with outside air as hot as 100 °F (38 °C). Humidity on such a day can be as low as 50 percent.
The weather handbook agrees. It says ice can form even under clear skies, with outside air as warm as 33 °C (90 °F) and relative humidity of 50 percent or more.
The Pilot's Handbook charts these conditions from 20 °F (-7 °C) to 100 °F (38 °C). Its caption still warns that icing is possible in conditions the chart does not show.

table.caption: Where the two FAA handbooks place carburettor icing, by outside air temperature and relative humidity.

article.heading: Why low power raises the risk
paragraphs: The ice builds where the cold is, around the throttle valve and in the venturi throat. It narrows the path for the fuel-air mixture, and the engine loses power. If enough builds up, the engine may stop.

Reduced power makes this worse. Close the throttle in flight and the engine cools quickly, and the fuel vaporises less completely than it would in a warm engine. The Pilot's Handbook says the engine is more prone to carburettor ice in that state.
Ice can form in any phase of flight. A descent at reduced power is when it is particularly dangerous. Under some conditions it can build unnoticed there and show itself only when you add power.
Size is no comfort either. The weather handbook says even a small amount of carburettor ice costs power and may make the engine run rough.

article.heading: How you notice it forming
paragraphs: With a fixed-pitch propeller, the first sign is a drop in engine rpm. Engine roughness may follow.
A constant-speed propeller changes its own pitch to make up for lost power, so it holds rpm steady. In that aircraft, the rpm will not show the ice.
Watch manifold pressure instead, the pressure in the intake manifold that carries the mixture to the combustion chambers. Carburettor ice shows there as a falling reading while rpm stays the same.

Whichever propeller you have, you are looking for lost power, and you may see it as lost altitude or airspeed. Vibration or roughness sometimes comes with it. Once you notice the loss, act at once to clear the ice that has formed and stop more from forming.

article.heading: How carburettor heat clears the ice
paragraphs: Engines with float-type carburettors carry a carburettor heat system for this. It is an anti-icing system that warms the air before it reaches the carburettor, to keep the fuel-air mixture above freezing. It can also melt ice that has already formed, as long as there is not too much.
When you find ice, apply full heat immediately and leave it on until you are sure the ice is gone. Partial heat, or heat left on too briefly, might make things worse.

Full heat cuts power further, and the engine may run rough as melted ice passes through. That can last from 30 seconds to several minutes. Resist easing the heat back, and keep it at full hot until normal power returns.

The rpm tells you whether there was ice. With a fixed-pitch propeller and ice present, rpm drops when the heat goes on, then slowly rises as the ice melts. With no ice, rpm drops and then holds steady.
With a constant-speed propeller, ice shows as a fall in manifold pressure and then a slow rise. With no ice, you see no rise until you turn the heat off.

article.heading: Using heat before the ice arrives
paragraphs: Prevention is the better use of carburettor heat, and you check that it works during the engine runup. If you suspect icing conditions and expect to close the throttle, set full heat first. Leave it on for as long as the throttle stays closed.
Every so often during that time, open the throttle smoothly for a few seconds. That keeps the engine warm, and without it the carburettor heater may not supply enough heat to stop ice forming.

Heat has a cost. Heated air is less dense, so engine power falls, sometimes by up to 15 percent, and the mixture gets richer. Because it cuts power and raises engine temperature, keep it off for takeoff and normal running unless checking for or clearing ice.
Some aircraft carry a carburettor air temperature gauge to help you spot icing conditions. Its face usually shows a yellow arc from -15 °C to +5 °C (5 °F to 41 °F), the range where icing may occur.
When the temperature and moisture make icing unlikely, the needle can sit in the yellow without harm. When conditions favour icing, use carburettor heat to keep it out of the arc.

posts.title: Acceleration that feels like a climb
posts.headline: With nothing to see outside, speeding up feels like pitching up.
posts.alt: Acceleration that feels like a climb: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With nothing to see outside, speeding up feels like pitching up. The picture shows a rendered Cessna 172 in clean left profile, seen level and square to its flank, high wing with visible struts and fixed tricycle gear, its nose pitched clearly down below level; a translucent outline of the same aeroplane overlapping it and sharing its tail position, pitched clearly nose-high, so the picture reads as one aeroplane in two attitudes rather than as two aircraft; a wide, obvious angle between the two noses, the ghost's high and the solid one's low, which is the subject of the picture; a thin pale line tracing the aeroplane's real path: up off the runway, over a shallow crest, then bending down toward the unlit water. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Why does forward acceleration feel like a nose-up pitch attitude?

Accelerate forward with no outside references and your sense of pitch says the nose came up. It did not, and the correction it invites is lowering the nose toward the surface. Nothing outside can settle it, so fly the pitch on the flight instruments and disregard what your body is reporting.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Forward acceleration can produce a false sensation of a nose-up pitch attitude.
Without outside visual references the pilot may lower the nose toward the surface, so pitch must be flown on the flight instruments rather than on what the body reports.
posts.intent: On a dark night takeoff, acceleration pushes the inner ear the same way a nose-up pitch would, and the instinct is to push down.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 17

figure_key.label: PITCH YOU FEEL
figure_key.points_at: The raised nose and spinner of the translucent ghost aeroplane.

figure_key.label: PITCH YOU ACTUALLY HAVE
figure_key.points_at: The solid aeroplane's nose, visibly below the ghost's and below level.

figure_key.label: NO HORIZON TO CHECK IT
figure_key.points_at: The place straight ahead of the spinner where black water meets sky with no seam.

figure_key.label: FLY THE INSTRUMENTS
figure_key.points_at: The solid aeroplane's windscreen and the warm instrument glow behind it.

article.heading: What happens on a dark night takeoff
paragraphs: Picture a night takeoff toward open water. You add full power, the aeroplane gathers speed, and the runway lights slide away behind you. Ahead of the windscreen there is nothing to look at.
Somewhere in the roll or the first part of the climb, your body tells you the nose has come up. It feels steep. The aeroplane has not pitched up at all.
The instinct that follows is to ease the stick forward and bring the nose down. That is the trap. The rest of this page walks through where the feeling comes from and why the answer is on the panel.

article.heading: Why speeding up feels like tilting back
paragraphs: Your inner ear holds the otolith organs. They are the part of your balance system that senses which way gravity and acceleration are pulling on your head.

Tilt your head backwards and the otolith organs register the change. A hard shove forward, like the one you get on a takeoff roll, stimulates them in the same way. From that signal alone, your brain cannot tell the two apart.
So it reports the familiar story. You feel yourself tilting back, which in an aeroplane means nose-up. This false sense of a raised nose from speeding up is called the somatogravic illusion.
The handbook uses takeoff as its example, because that is where a rapid acceleration is part of every flight. You meet the conditions for it every time you open the throttle.

figure.caption: Tilting your head back and speeding up forward send your inner ear the same message.
figure.alt: Tilting your head back and speeding up forward send your inner ear the same message.

article.heading: Why a dark night makes it worse
paragraphs: In daylight your eyes settle the question. You glance out, see the horizon where it should be, and know the nose is where you put it.

The illusion is most likely when visual references are poor. Over open water at night, black water meets black sky with no seam, and there is nothing to check the feeling against. The handbook names that exact case as flight without a visible horizon.
It lumps marginal visibility in with it, meaning visibility of less than 3 miles. In either case the inner ear becomes the loudest voice left in the cockpit.

Seat of the pants flying will not save you here. That means judging attitude from the pressure you feel through your seat, skin and muscles. Acceleration forces can overpower gravity, and then those signals go false as well.

article.heading: What the wrong correction does
paragraphs: Convinced the nose is high, a disoriented pilot pushes forward. The handbook says this can put the aeroplane into a nose-low attitude, or into a dive.
Just after takeoff you have very little height to give away. Lowering the nose there points the aeroplane at the surface you just left, while your body still insists you are climbing.

The illusion also runs in reverse. Pull the throttle back quickly and the rapid slowdown can have the opposite effect. The disoriented pilot then pulls the nose up, toward a nose-high attitude or a stall.

table.caption: The same sensor, fooled in both directions by a change in speed.
rows: Rapid acceleration, such as on takeoff
Pushes into a nose-low or dive attitude
Rapid deceleration from a quick throttle reduction
Pulls into a nose-up or stall attitude

article.heading: How to feel it safely with an instructor
paragraphs: You can meet this illusion on purpose. The handbook describes a demonstration called climbing while accelerating.

You close your eyes. Your instructor holds approach speed, straight and level, for several seconds. Then they speed up while keeping the aeroplane straight and level, and the usual sensation is that you are climbing.

A second exercise gets the same feeling from a turn. The instructor rolls slowly into a coordinated turn of about 1.5 positive G, approximately 50° of bank, and holds it for 90°. G is the load pressing you into your seat, and here it reads as a climb too.

Both exercises prove the same point. Your body's sense of attitude is often wrong, while the instruments are not fooled. Do them only at a safe height, with an instructor or a suitable safety pilot aboard.

article.heading: How to fly pitch on the instruments
paragraphs: Take pitch from the flight instruments, and treat what your body reports as noise. On a dark takeoff, set the attitude you want on the panel and hold it there. If the nose feels like it is climbing away, check the instruments before you touch the stick.

The false feeling is normal, and no amount of training makes it go away completely. What training does is teach you to override it. The more instrument flying you do, the less these illusions pull on you.
Get that training before you need it. The handbook says to get it before flying in visibility under 3 miles. The same goes for anywhere without a visible horizon, such as over open water at night.

Keep your head still during the takeoff, since sudden head movement is on the handbook's list of things to avoid. Arrive rested, too. Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, lost sleep and mild hypoxia, a shortage of oxygen, all make you easier to fool.

posts.title: Rotor cloud under a mountain wave
posts.headline: In a mountain wave, the roughest low-level air is under that smooth cloud.
posts.alt: Rotor cloud under a mountain wave: an illustrated diagram for pilots. In a mountain wave, the roughest low-level air is under that smooth cloud. The picture shows a mountain ridge in profile with the wind crossing it left to right; a smooth, hard-edged lens of lenticular cloud sitting at the wave crest downwind of the summit; a torn, ragged rotor cloud directly below that lenticular, at about ridge-top height; streamlines drawn unbroken from the lenticular down into the rotor, so the two clouds read as one wave. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: What's the difference between a lenticular cloud and a rotor cloud?

Air crossing a ridge can set up a standing wave downwind. Smooth lenticular cloud marks the crests. The rotor turns underneath, and down low that roll is usually the roughest part. The wave can be rough higher up too, so smooth cloud above is not a promise of smooth air.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: A mountain wave can form smooth lenticular cloud at its crests and turbulent rotor cloud beneath them.
At low level the rotor beneath the crests is usually the most turbulent part of the wave.
A mountain wave is often marked by lenticular and rotor clouds, but extremely severe wave winds can occur with little or no visual warning.
posts.intent: The smooth lenticular above and the ragged rotor below belong to the same wave, and down low the rotor is where the turbulence lives.

figure_key.label: SMOOTH EDGES MARK THE CREST
figure_key.points_at: The hard lit upper lip of the stacked lenticular cloud at the wave crest.

figure_key.label: ROTOR: USUALLY THE ROUGHEST
figure_key.points_at: The dark torn belly of the rotor cloud rolling directly beneath that lenticular.

figure_key.label: ONE WAVE, TWO DIFFERENT CLOUDS
figure_key.points_at: The streamline that runs unbroken from the lenticular crest down into the rotor roll.

article.heading: How a ridge sets the air waving
paragraphs: Picture a strong wind blowing across a mountain ridge on a stable day. Stable air resists being lifted, because once it is pushed up it is heavier than the air around it.

After the air clears the top of the ridge, gravity pulls it back down. Momentum carries it below its starting level, and compression warms it as it sinks, until it is lighter than the air around it. Up it goes again, overshoots again, and keeps bobbing downstream until the motion dies out.
That train of rises and falls is a mountain wave, and its high points are its crests. Air climbing toward a crest cools as it expands. With enough moisture, its water vapor condenses into cloud.

The cloud at a crest is a lenticular, named for its lens or airfoil shape. Lenticulars often line up in fairly straight bands parallel to the ridge but downwind of it, with clear sky between. Each band sits on a crest, so a row of them draws the wave for you.

article.heading: What a lenticular's edges tell you
paragraphs: The edges of a wave cloud give you a clue to the air inside it. Smooth, laminar edges and tops, meaning they look sleek and layered, go with little or no turbulence.

A lumpy, uneven cloud says the opposite. So does any sense that it is rolling around an axis running along the cloud. Lenticulars themselves can look either smooth or turbulent, so read each one on its own.
A smooth-looking lenticular layer can still be rough at the bottom. Inside the layer, the air typically runs from turbulent near its base to smooth near its top.

The wave also roughens the air at its crests and at its troughs, the low points between them. It moves strong wind up and down, which sharpens the wind shear, a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance. Shear like that stirs up turbulence.

article.heading: Why the air under the crest rolls
paragraphs: When a mountain wave is present, a rotor quite commonly forms on the downwind side of the mountain. A rotor is a horizontal roll of air that stays put, near or below ridge height, beneath a wave crest. With enough moisture, it shows up as a rotor cloud under the lenticular.

The rotor zone is an area of possibly severe to extreme wind shear and turbulence. Some references call shear severe when it shifts your airspeed by more than 15 kt. They also count a change in vertical speed of more than 500 feet per minute, or fpm.

The roughness comes with big changes in the wind below cloud level. Just downwind of the mountains, a strong shear layer often sits near the cloud base. It splits a turbulent wake below mountaintop height, the churned air behind the mountain, from the faster air above that carries the cloud.
The wind beneath lenticulars can swing and gust a lot, but it is usually not extremely strong. Pilots flying near these clouds often report moderate to severe turbulence underneath them.
Those cloud bases typically sit one to several thousand feet above ridge level. The rotor turns lower, near or below the ridge, and at that level it is usually the most turbulent part of the wave.

article.heading: Where the downslope windstorm ends
paragraphs: Rotors typically sit at the far end of a downslope windstorm. That is strong wind racing down the lee slope, the downwind side of the mountain, after the wave breaks high above. Gusts on those slopes can reach 100 kt.

That fast flow does not fade out gently. It often stops abruptly, some distance down the lee slope or well downwind of the mountains, and that stopping place is called the jump. When a rotor marks the end of the windstorm, it belongs to the jump itself.

Extreme turbulence often fills the jump, stretching 10,000 ft or more above the ground. A line of ragged rotor clouds sometimes marks it. Beyond the jump the air calms somewhat, but the turbulence can still be strong.

figure.caption: The rotor line sits over the jump, where the fast wind down the lee slope ends and extreme turbulence is frequent.
figure.alt: The rotor line sits over the jump, where the fast wind down the lee slope ends and extreme turbulence is frequent.

article.heading: How to spot a rotor cloud early
paragraphs: A rotor and its cloud are usually spinning hard. From a moving airplane, though, you may not see the spin until you are quite close.
From far off, a rotor cloud can pass for a harmless cumulus, the billowy cloud of a sunny afternoon. Look at its downwind side. It is typically rounded in the direction the rotor turns.
Then look along the bottom for ragged tags or streamers of cloud. They seem to form and vanish quickly, and that flicker is what gives you a sense of the spin inside.

article.heading: What a rotor does to your airplane
paragraphs: The advice on rotor zones is to stay out of them. Strong turbulence is likely around a rotor, most of all on its upwind side.
The spinning air can also produce rolling moments, forces that bank the airplane, stronger than your controls can counter. That can end in a loss of control.
Low altitude is where a rotor is most dangerous, and takeoff and landing top the list. You are slow then, and the airplane is set up for relatively high drag.

Close to the runway in mountain winds, local gusts above 50 kt are possible, with downdrafts greater than 1,500 fpm. A downdraft can sink you faster than your airplane can climb. Airplanes with high wing and power loading, meaning lots of weight for their wing and engine, are most exposed.

table.caption: Low-level wind figures for flying near mountains, from FAA-H-8083-28 chapters 16 and 19.
rows: Suspect disturbances downwind of rugged terrain
10,000 ft or more above the surface

article.heading: When the wave leaves no clouds
paragraphs: Lenticulars and rotor clouds need enough moisture in the air arriving at the mountain. Mountain waves often come with them, or with blowing dust. That is not always so, and extremely severe winds can arrive with little or no visual warning.
So a clear sky downwind of a ridge does not mean there is no wave. Trapped lee waves, waves whose energy stays below a certain height, frequently occur without any cloud.

Watch the wind instead. Suspect hidden disturbances whenever you fly downwind of rugged terrain with ridge-level wind above about 20 kt. That figure is the prevailing wind at the ridge crest, upwind of you, not a local gust.

Fly low over mountains with 20 kt or more at ridge level and you can expect moderate or greater turbulence. You can also expect strong updrafts and downdrafts, and very strong rotor and shear zones. That holds most of all for general aviation airplanes, the kind you likely train in.

The worst mountain wind events tend to fall between late autumn and early spring, when the big weather-map winds blow hardest. In a wave flow, fly at turbulence penetration speed, the speed meant for rough air. Stay clear of terrain that drops away sharply, even with no lenticular in sight.

posts.title: The fuel you cannot use
posts.headline: Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold.
posts.alt: The fuel you cannot use: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold. The picture shows a rendered low-wing single-engine aeroplane in level cruise, solid and fully lit, with a thin pale track line running forward from the spinner and stopping in open air; a translucent dimmed ghost of the same aeroplane further along that same track line, with open air between the solid aircraft and the ghost; a cut-away section through the wing fuel tank lifted large into the near foreground, joined to the wing root by one thin line; fuel brimmed to the filler neck inside that cut-away, its upper surface clearly the top of what the tank holds. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold.
Full explainer with the FAA sources it rests on flightdecide.com/e/fuel-cannot
teaches: An aircraft's total fuel capacity includes an unusable quantity that cannot be relied on in flight.
Fuel planning uses the usable figure from the approved flight manual.
posts.intent: Usable fuel is less than total fuel, and the difference is a published number rather than a rounding error.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 10
Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 7

figure_key.label: TRAPPED BELOW THE PICKUP

article.heading: What a full tank does not tell you
paragraphs: You fill the tanks to the top of the filler neck and cap them. The number printed on the tank, or on the fuel gauge placard, is the total the tanks hold. Some of that fuel will never reach the engine.

That leftover share is called unusable fuel, the fuel that stays in the tanks and lines and cannot be relied on in flight. Whatever is left after you take it away is usable fuel, the fuel the engine can actually burn.

Pilots often treat the gap between the two as a rounding error. It is not. The manufacturer measures it and publishes it for your aircraft type. A full tank tells you what you carry, and the usable figure tells you what you can burn.

article.heading: Why some fuel never reaches the engine
paragraphs: Fuel has a long way to travel before it burns. In a fuel-injected engine it leaves the tank and passes through an engine-driven fuel pump. Then it goes to a fuel-air control unit, which does the job a carburetor would do.

From there the fuel runs to a fuel manifold, the valve that splits it between cylinders. Discharge nozzles in each cylinder head then spray it into the intake ports. An auxiliary fuel pump backs up the engine-driven pump for starting and emergencies.

The whole chain draws from the tank through an outlet called the pickup. Fuel lying below that outlet, or trapped in the shape of the tank floor, cannot be drawn into the lines. It is still fuel, and it still shows as part of the total, but the engine cannot use it.

article.heading: Where the usable number comes from
paragraphs: You do not work out unusable fuel yourself. The manufacturer establishes it, and it is written in the approved flight manual for your aircraft. That manual is called the airplane flight manual (AFM) or the pilot's operating handbook (POH).

This is the same place the manufacturer publishes other limits you must respect. The fore and aft limits for the center of gravity, the balance point of the loaded aircraft, sit in the AFM or POH. They also appear in the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), the aircraft's official specification.

Look in the fuel section of your AFM or POH. You will find total capacity and usable capacity listed as separate figures. Two aircraft that look alike on the ramp can carry different numbers, so read the manual for the one you are flying.

article.heading: What the unusable fuel still costs you
paragraphs: Unusable fuel gives you no range, but it does not weigh nothing. Gasoline weighs 6 pounds per gallon. Every gallon trapped in the tank is 6 pounds you carry for the whole flight.

Weight matters because too much of it hurts nearly every part of performance. An overloaded aircraft needs a longer takeoff run and climbs more slowly. It also stalls at a higher speed and needs a longer landing roll.

During a flight, burning fuel is normally the only change in weight. As the usable fuel goes, the aircraft gets lighter and performs better. The unusable fuel stays aboard, so it counts as weight from engine start to shutdown.

Where fuel sits also affects balance. If you feed the engine unevenly from tanks on one side, the aircraft becomes wing-heavy. Holding it level with trim or control pressure adds drag and wastes fuel you had planned to use.

article.heading: What happens when the plan uses total fuel
paragraphs: Picture two plans for the same trip. One divides the total capacity by the fuel burn. The other divides the usable capacity. The first plan promises you minutes of flight that the tanks cannot deliver.

When the usable fuel runs out, the engine stops getting fuel even though the tanks are not dry. That is fuel starvation, the engine quitting because fuel no longer reaches it. The gauge and the tank may both suggest fuel is still aboard.

Restarting is not a sure thing either. Fuel-injected engines have a known weakness here. Restarting one that quit from fuel starvation brings its own problems, so an engine that stops this way does not reliably come back.

article.heading: How to plan from the usable figure
paragraphs: Start every fuel calculation with the usable capacity from the AFM or POH, never the total. If the tanks are not full, work out how much usable fuel is actually aboard. Only that quantity goes into your time and range sums.

Treat the usable figure as a ceiling, not a target. Your plan should land with fuel still in the tanks, including the reserve the regulations require. Those reserve rules come from the regulations, and the source here does not give their figures.

Carrying less fuel to save weight is a fair choice, but it trades away range. If you remove fuel to get under a weight limit, redo the fuel plan with the smaller usable quantity. Then check the new figure still covers the trip and the reserve.

posts.title: Ground effect in the flare
posts.headline: Your drag falls away inside the last wingspan.
posts.alt: Ground effect in the flare: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your drag falls away inside the last wingspan. The picture shows a rendered light single nose-high in the flare, wings level, main wheels hovering a few feet above the runway centreline; a ticked vertical dimension line one wingspan tall from the low aircraft's wingtip to the asphalt, with the aeroplane sitting well inside it; ghost comparison: the same aeroplane in the same nose-high attitude, a pale unfilled outline about one and a half wingspans higher and slightly behind; tip trails behind the low aircraft pressed wide and shallow along the asphalt, while the ghost's trails curl into two deep, tight vortices. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Throttle closed, the nose where you set it, and the airplane keeps flying down the runway.
Come within a wingspan of the surface and the wing enters ground effect. Induced drag goes down. The airplane holds off, and the runway keeps going by.
The same thing happens on takeoff. You can be airborne below normal flying speed, then settle back as you climb out of the last wingspan.
FlightDecide computes your takeoff weight from the fuel you loaded.
Full explainer with the FAA sources it rests on https://flightdecide.com/explainers/ground-effect-in-the-flare/
When somebody asks why you floated, what is the one word in your answer?
teaches: Within about one wingspan of the surface, ground effect reduces induced drag and the thrust required to hold a low airspeed in level flight.
The reduced drag is why an aircraft floats in the flare and why it can lift off below normal flying speed and settle back.
posts.intent: Within about one wingspan of the surface induced drag falls away, so the aeroplane floats on air that has nowhere to go.

article.heading: What you feel just before touchdown
paragraphs: You've closed the throttle and eased the nose up for the flare, the gentle pitch-up just before touchdown. Now you're waiting for the wheels to touch, but the runway keeps sliding past and the airplane keeps flying just above it. It doesn't seem to want to come down.

Pilots have noticed this since the first flights, and it feels like a cushion of air trapped under the wing. Its name is ground effect, the change in airflow around an airplane flying close to the ground or water.

Ground effect normally reaches up to about one wingspan above the surface. Inside that height the wing loses part of its induced drag, the drag that comes with making lift. With less drag to slow it, the airplane gives up its speed slowly and floats.

article.heading: Where induced drag comes from
paragraphs: A wing holds the airplane up by pushing air downward. The air streaming down behind the wing is called downwash, and the harder the wing works, the more of it there is.

The air under the wing is at higher pressure than the air above it. Near each tip it flows sideways around the edge and rolls up into a spinning tube called a wingtip vortex. Making the downwash and the vortices takes energy, and that energy is paid for as induced drag.

Slow flight makes it worse. To hold the airplane up at lower speed you need a higher angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air. A higher angle means a bigger pressure difference, stronger vortices and more induced drag.

Induced drag rises as the inverse square of airspeed, so slowing down makes it grow fast. At high speed, parasite drag, the drag of moving the airframe itself through the air, makes up most of the total. In the flare you are slow, so induced drag is the part that dominates.

article.heading: What the runway does to the airflow
paragraphs: Now bring that wing down near the runway. The air it pushes down has nowhere to go, because the surface blocks its path downward. The ground is interfering with the airflow, and that interference is ground effect.
That blocked flow weakens the upwash, the air rising to meet the front of the wing. It weakens the downwash behind the wing and the wingtip vortices too.

Smaller vortices change how lift is spread along the span, and induced drag falls. The wing now needs a lower angle of attack to make the same lift. Hold the old angle and it makes more lift than it did.

article.heading: How close the wing has to be
paragraphs: As you descend through that last wingspan, ground effect grows, and most of it arrives very close to the runway. The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge gives the figures.
With the wing one wingspan above the ground, induced drag drops by only 1.4 percent. At 1/4 of the span the drop is 23.5 percent. At 1/10 of the span it is 47.6 percent, close to half.
The Airplane Flying Handbook rounds those two lower figures to about 25 percent and about 50 percent. Either way, the big saving only comes with the wing very near the surface.

So one wingspan marks where ground effect can first be detected, and the lower heights show where it does real work. Because the saving sits so low, you notice it most just after lift-off and just before touchdown.

figure.caption: Induced drag barely changes at one wingspan up, but nearly half of it is gone by 1/10 of the span.
figure.alt: Induced drag barely changes at one wingspan up, but nearly half of it is gone by 1/10 of the span.

article.heading: Why extra speed becomes a long float
paragraphs: Back in the flare, you hold a steady nose-up attitude at low speed, just off the runway. Those are exactly the conditions where ground effect is strongest.
Thrust required, the push needed to hold a speed in level flight, is parasite drag and induced drag added together. Ground effect cuts the induced part, so thrust required drops sharply at low speed.

With the power off, drag is what slows you down. Take a big share of it away and the airplane loses speed slowly. Any extra speed you carry into the flare can then become a long float down the runway.
The lift changes too. If the wing arrives in ground effect at the same angle of attack, it makes more lift and the airplane can float.
So as you near the ground at the end of the approach, you take some power off. Leave it in and the airplane will tend to climb.

article.heading: Why a slow lift-off can settle back
paragraphs: On takeoff the same physics runs the other way. The roll, the lift-off and the start of the climb all happen inside ground effect, where induced drag is reduced. That can make the airplane seem ready to fly well below its recommended takeoff speed.

Your instruments read differently here too. Ground effect usually raises the pressure at the static source, the port that feeds the airspeed indicator and altimeter, so both read slightly low. You can be airborne at an indicated airspeed below the one normally needed.

Climb out of ground effect and all of this reverses. The wing needs a higher angle of attack for the same lift, and induced drag and thrust required both rise. The nose tends to pitch up, stability decreases, and the airspeed indicator reads higher as static pressure falls.

If you lifted off short of speed, that extra drag arrives as you leave ground effect. Your climb will be much weaker than at Vy, the best rate of climb speed, or even Vx, the best angle of climb speed.

The worst case is a heavy airplane on a hot day at high density altitude, where the air is thin. There the airplane can lift off yet be unable to climb out of ground effect and settle back onto the runway. So you never force it into the air before the manufacturer's recommended takeoff speed.

article.heading: Using ground effect on purpose
paragraphs: Ground effect also has its uses. With a long enough runway or no obstacles, the reduced drag can help the airplane accelerate after lift-off.

A soft-field takeoff is built around it. Tall grass, soft sand, mud and snow drag at the wheels, so you hold the nose high and let the wing lift the airplane off early. It leaves the ground below a safe climb speed, held up by ground effect.

Once airborne, you lower the nose gently and let it accelerate with the wheels just clear of the surface. If it rises out of ground effect too soon, it tends to settle back even at full power. So you keep it in ground effect until it reaches at least Vx.

Some airplanes tend to lift off well before Vx on a short field. It is better to let one lift off and hold it level, wheels just clear, until it reaches Vx. Pinning it to the runway with forward pressure overloads the nosewheel and slows the acceleration.

posts.title: A narrow runway and a low approach
posts.headline: A narrow runway hides how low you really are.
posts.alt: A narrow runway and a low approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A narrow runway hides how low you really are. The picture shows the runway seen obliquely ahead, its paved width visibly narrow with the edges close together and the markings small and crowded; a pale unfilled outline of the usual, wider runway drawn around the real one, so the gap between true edge and outline can be read; ghost outline of the same aeroplane on the normal approach path, at the same distance out and clearly above the solid one; solid aeroplane low on a shallower path, sitting close to the ground short of the threshold. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: You're on short final at a field you've never used, and the picture out the windscreen looks normal.

The runway ahead is narrower than the ones you learned on. A runway narrower than usual creates the illusion of extra height. That is the narrow runway illusion, and it needs nothing more than the width you're looking at. The picture says come down.

Miss it and the approach goes low. Objects along the approach path start to matter, and landing short is the other end of the same mistake. The Aeronautical Information Manual files it at 8-1-5, with the rest of the illusions of flight.
FlightDecide reads the NOTAMs for your destination and flags runway and obstruction notices in the briefing.
Next time you brief an unfamiliar field, look up its runway width and compare it to your home runway.
Check the current CFR before you apply this to a real flight.
teaches: A runway narrower than usual creates the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it actually is.
A pilot who does not recognise the illusion flies a lower-than-normal approach, with the risk of striking objects along the approach path or landing short.
posts.intent: A narrower runway than you are used to makes you feel higher than you are, and the uncorrected result is an approach that is too low.

article.heading: What a narrow runway does to your eyes
paragraphs: Most of your landings have been at one airport, on one runway. Today you're on final somewhere new, and the strip ahead is clearly narrower than the one you know.
A runway narrower than you're used to can make you feel higher above the ground than you really are. The FAA calls this the runway width illusion.

The FAA's Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge says the effect is strongest when the two runways' length-to-width relationships are comparable. Nothing about the view looks wrong. It just tells you that you have height to spare.

article.heading: Why feeling high makes you fly low
paragraphs: If you think you're high, you fix it the way you were taught. The Airplane Flying Handbook says you steepen an approach that looks too high by cutting power and lowering the nose.
Except you weren't high. Once you've corrected for height you never had, you're on a lower-than-normal approach path, the line your aeroplane is really flying down toward the runway.

The AIM is firm about the outcome. A pilot who doesn't recognise the illusion will fly a lower approach. The word that matters is recognise, because the pilots it catches are the ones who aren't expecting it.

article.heading: What a low approach puts in your way
paragraphs: A low path brings you closer to everything short of the runway. The AIM names two risks. You can hit objects along the approach path, or you can land short, touching down before the runway begins.

If you find yourself low and undershooting, the handbook says to raise the nose and add power to level off, holding the correct airspeed. When you reach the glide path you want, reduce power and lower the nose to stay on it.

Trying to stretch the approach by raising the nose without adding power is almost always a bad idea, the handbook warns. If you're very low, you may not manage a stabilized approach at all, meaning one flown at a constant angle toward a chosen point. Then the normal answer is a go-around.

article.heading: A wide runway fools you the other way
paragraphs: The same illusion runs in reverse. A runway wider than you're used to can make you feel lower than you are.
The FAA's runway illusion figure says this leads to a higher approach. The AIM lists what goes wrong next. You may level off too high and land hard, or overshoot the runway.
Knowing both directions helps. Every new airport gets measured against your home runway, whether you want it to or not.

table.caption: The runway width illusion in both directions, from the FAA's runway illusion figure and the AIM
rows: Striking objects along the approach path, or landing short
Levelling out high and landing hard, or overshooting the runway

article.heading: How to read the runway picture
paragraphs: Start with the aiming point, the spot on the ground your aeroplane is heading straight for. On a steady descent it seems to stay put. It doesn't slide under the nose, and it doesn't creep away ahead of you.

Keep an eye on the gap between the aiming point and the horizon. At a constant angle that gap stays the same. If the aiming point rises toward the horizon, the point you'll really reach is closer than you think.

The runway's shape gives clues too. From final it looks like a trapezoid, and on a stabilized approach it keeps the same shape as it grows. A shallower approach makes it look shorter and wider. A steeper one makes it look longer and narrower.

Don't stare at one spot. The handbook suggests scanning from the aiming point to the horizon, to objects along the runway, to an area well short of it, and back again. It's easier to spot a drift off the path when your eyes keep moving.

figure.caption: As the approach angle changes, the runway's outline changes too, so a runway that's getting shorter and wider means your path is getting shallower.
figure.alt: As the approach angle changes, the runway's outline changes too, so a runway that's getting shorter and wider means your path is getting shallower.

article.heading: Cross-checks that don't depend on width
paragraphs: Expect illusions before you arrive at an unfamiliar airport, especially at night or in bad weather. Look at the airport diagram and the Chart Supplement U.S., the FAA's airport directory, for runway slope, terrain and lighting. If you can, look the airport over from the air before you land.

On every approach, day or night, check the altimeter often. Use a Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI) or Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI) whenever one is there. Both are lighting systems that give you a visual reference for the descent.

On an instrument approach, use the electronic glideslope if there is one. On nonprecision approaches, use the visual descent point (VDP) printed on many charts. None of these depends on how wide the runway looks.
Watch out for distraction as well. The handbook says the chance of an approach accident goes up when an emergency or some other task pulls you away from your usual routine.

posts.title: The black hole approach
posts.headline: Over dark ground you fly lower than you think.
posts.alt: The black hole approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With nothing lit below, you fly lower than intended. The picture shows night side elevation with the lit runway small and far in the right third and the approach entering from the left; solid aeroplane on the lower, shallower path, visibly close to the dark surface short of the field; ghost outline of the same aeroplane on the intended path at the same distance out, clearly above the solid one; completely unlit ground or water between the aeroplane and the threshold, with no towns, roads or scattered lights. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: You turn final over the bay, and the only lights anywhere are the ones on the runway.

Night approaches over unlit terrain or water have a name. The black hole approach. The cues you use to judge height and distance are gone. No roads or rooflines under the nose. Only the runway lights, sitting out there alone.

On a lit approach the picture corrects you the whole way down. Over black ground it never updates. A small sink goes unchallenged. The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge files it with the visual illusions in chapter 17.
FlightDecide reads your destination NOTAMs for the planned window, runway lighting outages included.
If the ground below the approach shows nothing, what is left to tell you how high you are?
teaches: An approach over unlit terrain or water removes the visual cues normally used to judge height and distance.
With no surrounding ground features, the aircraft can seem higher than it actually is.
The result tends toward an approach lower than intended.
In the worst case, the aircraft lands short of the runway.
Bright runway lights with few lights around them can do the opposite, making the runway seem closer and leading to a higher approach.
posts.intent: With no lit features between you and the runway there is no visual slope information, so the approach is flown on an impression.

article.heading: What a dark final looks like
paragraphs: Picture a night approach to a runway on the shore, with the whole final leg over open water. Ahead are two lines of edge lights and a row of threshold lights. Below and around you, nothing is lit at all.

On a daytime approach you judge height from many small clues. Fields, trees, roads and buildings grow larger as you descend and slide past the edge of your view. Over black water or unlit ground, every one of those clues is gone.
Nothing about the scene feels alarming. The runway looks clear and bright, and the approach seems easy.
This is the black hole approach. It happens when you land from over water or unlit terrain and the runway lights are the only source of light.

article.heading: Why you feel higher than you are
paragraphs: Normally the ground around the runway helps you judge how high you are and how far you have to go. Part of that comes from peripheral cues, the things you notice at the edge of your vision.

Without those cues, the handbook says, orientation is difficult. Your eyes still hand you an answer, and it tends to be wrong. With nothing around the runway to compare against, the airplane seems higher than it actually is.
Water is the classic case, but it is not the only one. Unlit land does the same, and so does terrain left blank by snow. What matters is that there is nothing on the ground to read.
The runway itself can look out of place as well. It can seem to slope down away from you, or slope up toward you.

article.heading: How that ends up short of the runway
paragraphs: When the picture tells you that you are high, you correct for it by descending. The correction feels right, because it makes the view look the way you expect.
The result is an approach lower than you meant to fly. From the seat nothing looks wrong, because the error is in the picture you are flying by.
Over water or unlit land there is nothing between you and the threshold to warn you. In the worst case, the airplane lands short of the runway.
Your eyes are not failing here. They are doing their normal job with far too little to work on, so the approach ends up flown on an impression.

article.heading: When bright runway lights push you high
paragraphs: The lights around a runway can bend the error the other way. Picture a runway with bright edge and approach lights, and very few lights on the ground around it.

Bright lights make a runway look closer than it is. The handbook says this setup can create the illusion of being lower, or of having less distance to go. A pilot who misses it tends to fly a higher approach.
Now change the ground under you. Flying over terrain with only a few lights makes the runway seem to recede, or look farther away. Here the tendency is a lower than normal approach.

A city in the distance on higher ground beyond the runway also tends to pull you low. So the same dark night can push you high or low, depending on what is lit in front of you. Neither error is safe to assume.

Aircraft seems higher than it actually is
Terrain with only a few lights

article.heading: Where to expect it
paragraphs: The classic setting is an airport by the water, approached from over the water at night. The handbook also points to airports in sparsely populated areas, where there are few if any surface references.
A missing horizon or surface reference is common over water, at night and in low visibility. When all three stack up on one final, you have the conditions for this illusion.
Airports you have never flown into deserve the most suspicion. Go in expecting to be fooled, especially at night or in poor weather.

Before the flight, read the airport diagram and the Chart Supplement, which used to be called the Airport/Facility Directory. Both tell you about runway slope, the terrain around the field and the lighting. Knowing the layout and boundaries before you start down helps you hold a safe approach angle.

article.heading: What to fly by instead of the view
paragraphs: Since the view is what misleads you, judge the slope with something that does not depend on it. If there is an electronic glide slope, a descent path you follow on your instruments rather than by eye, use it.

If the runway has a visual approach slope indicator, or VASI, use that as well. It is a lighting aid at the runway that gives you a visual reference for the slope, and the handbook says to use it whenever one is available.

Where neither exists, your flight instruments help you keep your orientation and fly a normal approach. The handbook's wider advice on illusions is to rely on the instruments over what your senses report.
If at any point you doubt your altitude or your position relative to the runway, do not press on. The handbook's instruction is to go around.
Practice is part of it too. The handbook recommends keeping night currency and proficiency, flying both cross-country and local operations at a range of airfields.

posts.title: Attention narrowing under fatigue
posts.headline: Fatigue narrows your scan before you feel impaired.
posts.alt: Attention narrowing under fatigue: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Fatigue narrows your scan before you feel impaired. The picture shows side elevation of a single-engine aeroplane in profile left of centre, late in the day, with layered ridgelines stepping back to the right into haze; a narrow pale-edged cone of attention opening forward from the cockpit, reaching only one small lit notch of rock at the shoulder of the pass; ghost comparison: a thin unfilled outline of a far wider cone from the same point, spanning nearly the whole forward view, the scan the pilot believes is being flown; terrain inside the narrow cone crisp and readable, everything between its edges and the ghost outline dimmed and softened into haze. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Fourth hour in the airplane, you copy a squawk code and look up to find the heading off the bug.

Fatigue does that. It degrades attention, and it takes away the ability to divide attention between two jobs. Whatever your hands are doing wins. The instrument you were watching a minute ago goes unwatched, and nothing announces it.

You can't feel the narrowing while it's happening. Chapter 2 of the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge covers why fitness gets judged against a written checklist. The same tired brain does the self-assessment, and it reports back that everything is fine.
FlightDecide reads the TAFs and NOTAMs across your whole planned window, so late-day workload is visible early.
On a long day, the checklist is the only honest opinion in the cockpit.
teaches: Fatigue degrades attention and the ability to divide it between tasks.
Fatigue is hard to judge from how you feel: a pilot who has flown 16 hours may still say they are not too tired, so the IMSAFE checklist helps identify it.
posts.intent: Fatigue narrows the field of attention before it feels like impairment, so the scan stops covering what you think it covers.

article.heading: What fatigue takes from your attention
paragraphs: Picture the last leg of a long day. You're holding altitude and the radio calls go out on time. Nothing feels wrong, so you assume your attention is where it always is.
Fatigue degrades your attention and your concentration. It also impairs coordination and makes you worse at communicating. Together these seriously weaken your ability to make good decisions.
It can be physical or mental. Sleep loss, exercise or physical work bring on the physical kind, while stress and long stretches of mental work bring on the other.
For your scan, attention matters most, especially your ability to divide it between several jobs at once. Flying asks for that split on every leg.

article.heading: Why your scan shrinks toward the middle
paragraphs: Skill fatigue, a type of acute or short-term fatigue, shows up in how you fly. Its first effect is on timing, with each step of a task slightly off while the whole looks normal. You end up flying the steps as separate pieces instead of one smooth action.

Its second effect narrows what you see. Your attention settles on movements and objects in the center of your vision, and the periphery, the outer part of your view, gets neglected. Your control inputs lose accuracy and smoothness along with it.

Exhaustion on a night flight pushes the same way. A worn-out pilot tends to work one aspect of a situation and miss the total of what it needs. Instead of a proper scan, you may fixate on the instruments or stare off, and stop handling several tasks.

Taken far enough, this becomes fixation, locking your attention on one goal or object while ignoring the cues that show your orientation. It tends to set in while you concentrate on the instruments or on a landing. You lock onto one task and forget to look at what is going on around you.
That is how traffic gets missed. Whether you spot an aircraft on a collision course depends partly on where you are looking.

article.heading: Why one task crowds out the rest
paragraphs: Fatigue, like stress or work overload, can lock you onto one item that seems important. Your awareness of the rest of the flight shrinks around it.

Distractions often start small. A gauge that is not reading right draws you in, and you stop monitoring the instruments and scanning outside. Control of the airplane is what slips while you work on it.

Workload makes it worse. As it climbs, you can no longer give attention to several tasks at one time, and you may begin to focus on one. At task saturation, having more to do than you can take in, input from other sources stops registering.

So fatigue removes the very skill a busy cockpit calls for, which is dividing your attention. Tasks also increase significantly in the landing phase, where the flying calls for more precision and attention.

figure.caption: When task requirements rise above what a pilot can handle, some tasks are done poorly and others are not done at all.
figure.alt: When task requirements rise above what a pilot can handle, some tasks are done poorly and others are not done at all.

article.heading: How a long night flight adds to it
paragraphs: Stack late nights and fatigue on sustained flight above 5,000 feet, and you may grow less discerning and less decisive. You may also question information less and become more compliant and accepting.
The timing makes it dangerous. Take a night instrument approach in the weather after a 4-hour flight, the most demanding stretch of the trip. It arrives when your guard is down the most.

By the end of a long flight day, fatigue and low-altitude hypoxia, too little oxygen for the body, have drained much of your energy. The handbook describes the result as a shift from deciding to accepting.

Your eyes take a hit as well. Above 4,000 feet pressure altitude, night vision drops measurably unless you are on supplemental oxygen, and fatigue makes the loss worse. At 12,000 feet at night, parts of your normal vision may be missing or out of focus.

article.heading: Why feeling fine tells you little
paragraphs: Ask a fatigued pilot who has flown 16 hours if they are too tired to keep flying. The answer may be no.
Flying alone, you act as your own quality control. The tired mind that is missing things is the same one judging whether it is missing them.
Most pilots are goal oriented. Offered a flight, they tend to deny their own limits and give weight to things that have no bearing on the trip.

That makes fatigue one of the hardest hazards to catch, since it may not be apparent until you have made serious errors. Fatigued pilots have fallen asleep while flying, yet the effects may be subtle, such as dulled thinking and weaker decisions.

article.heading: How IMSAFE asks the question for you
paragraphs: Since feel is unreliable, use a checklist that asks the question for you. IMSAFE is a self-check for before every flight, and it stands for Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Emotion.

The fatigue item asks whether you are tired and not adequately rested. Too little sleep is one cause, so start with how you slept rather than how you feel. Hypoxia and your emotional state can both intensify it.

Rest and 8 hours of sound sleep ordinarily cure acute fatigue. Sleep only corrects that kind, though. Chronic fatigue, which lasts over a long period, can involve several factors and needs more analysis and a remedy of its own.
The check does not stop at takeoff. On any flight longer than 2 hours, run the 5 P check, a review that includes you as the pilot, every hour.

posts.title: Stall speed rising with bank angle
posts.headline: Steepen a level turn and your stall speed rises.
posts.alt: Stall speed rising with bank angle: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A steeper level turn raises your stall speed. The picture shows a rendered single-engine aircraft heeled hard over in a steep turn, wings near sixty degrees of bank; the nose held on the horizon so the steep turn reads as level, not descending; a pale ghost of the same aircraft in a shallow bank, wings close to level; a thin level reference line joining solid aircraft and ghost at the same altitude. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Halfway around the steep turn the horn chirps, and the airspeed needle hasn't moved.

The wing is holding you up and hauling you around the corner at the same time. In a level turn, load factor grows with bank angle. Stall speed follows the square root of that load. Same airplane, higher number.

That number never shows up on the panel. The needle reads the same as it did wings level, so the margin feels unchanged. It has shrunk. The Airplane Flying Handbook works through steep turns in chapter 5.
FlightDecide computes the weight and balance for your planned load, so the gross weight behind your published stall speeds is a number you already have.
Next steep turns with your instructor, note the speed where the buffet starts and compare it to the wings level figure.
teaches: In a level turn load factor increases with bank angle.
Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor, so a 60 degree level turn doubles the load and raises the stall speed by about 41 percent.
posts.intent: A level turn raises load factor and the stall speed rises with the square root of it, so a steep turn stalls at a higher speed.

article.heading: Why a steep turn stalls sooner
paragraphs: Picture yourself holding altitude at a steady airspeed and rolling into a 60 degree bank. The airspeed has not changed. Yet the airplane is now closer to a stall than it was a moment ago.

The reason is the extra work the wing is doing. In a level turn it has to hold up the airplane's weight and pull it around the corner at the same time. The steeper the bank, the harder the wing works.
That extra work has a name, load factor, and the stall speed rises with it. At 60 degrees of bank, the FAA's Airplane Flying Handbook puts the rise at 41 percent over the wings level stall speed.

article.heading: What load factor means
paragraphs: Load factor is the load the wing carries compared with the airplane's weight. Flying straight and level, the wing carries exactly the weight, and that is 1G. At 2G the wing is carrying twice the weight.
In a turn, the wing's lift tilts with the airplane. Part of it now points toward the center of the turn and pulls you around. Only the rest is left pointing up against the weight.

To stay level, you ask the wing for more lift in total. The more you bank, the more of that lift goes sideways, and the more total lift you need. So in a level turn, load factor grows with bank angle.

In a coordinated, level 60 degree bank, the load factor is 2G. Coordinated means the ball in the slip/skid indicator is centered. The wing is now holding up twice the airplane's weight at the same airspeed.

figure.caption: In the bank, the tilted lift has to grow to twice the weight so that its upward part still matches the weight.
figure.alt: In the bank, the tilted lift has to grow to twice the weight so that its upward part still matches the weight.

article.heading: How the square root sets the number
paragraphs: Stall speed does not rise at the same rate as load factor. It rises with the square root of the load factor. So when the load doubles, the stall speed goes up by 41 percent rather than doubling.
That softens the jump, but only a little. A 41 percent rise is a big change to a number that is easy to treat as fixed.

Take the wings level stall speed you learned for your own airplane. In a coordinated, level 60 degree bank, the stall comes at that figure plus 41 percent. The handbook gives no stall speed for any one airplane, so do the sum with yours.

table.caption: The same airplane at the same airspeed, wings level and in a level 60 degree turn.

article.heading: Why the stall follows angle of attack
paragraphs: To make that extra lift at the same airspeed, you raise the angle of attack. Angle of attack is the angle at which the wing's chord, a straight line from leading to trailing edge, meets the oncoming air.
As that angle grows, lift grows and so does drag. Each wing has a limit to that angle. Beyond it, the airflow separates from the top surface, lift drops and drag climbs. That is a stall.
The handbook is firm here. A stall comes from exceeding that limiting angle, not from a lack of airspeed. Stall speed is only the airspeed at which you reach the limit under one set of conditions.

In a 2G turn you are already holding a higher angle of attack than you did wings level. You sit closer to the limit, and so closer to the higher stall speed. That is why the handbook says you can stall at any airspeed, in any attitude and at any power setting.

Load factor is one of several things that set stall speed. Gross weight, center of gravity and flap setting move it too. Stall speed is not a constant, and the handbook wants you to understand what moves it.

article.heading: What changes when you are already slow
paragraphs: In slow flight practice you fly a target speed just above the stall warning. The handbook suggests 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed. That margin is measured against a wings level stall.
At that speed, any further increase in angle of attack or load factor, or any cut in power, brings a stall warning. Rolling into a steeper bank is exactly that kind of load factor increase.
Put the two numbers side by side. Your margin was 5 to 10 knots over the 1G stall speed. Steepen the bank and the stall speed itself climbs toward the speed you are flying.
Reduced airspeeds are normal on takeoff and departure, and on approach and landing. Those are also the phases flown close to the ground. A turn there adds load factor to a speed that was already low.

article.heading: What the airplane tells you first
paragraphs: A stall warning comes before the stall itself. It shows up as buffet, a shaking you feel through the airframe, or as the stall horn sounding.
The handbook says to react to and correct for any stall indication. A stall can lead to loss of control if the angle of attack is not reduced.

The stall speeds you learn for your airplane are 1G figures for one weight and configuration. In a steep level turn, the warning arrives at a speed that would give you room to spare wings level. Knowing why keeps it from being a surprise.
The aim, in slow flight and in turns, is to maneuver without setting off the stall warning at all. Knowing that 60 degrees of bank means 2G and a 41 percent higher stall speed is what lets you do it.

posts.title: Losing the headwind on final
posts.headline: A decreasing headwind costs airspeed and drops you below the path.
posts.alt: Losing the headwind on final: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A decreasing headwind costs airspeed and drops you below the path. The picture shows two wind layers divided by a soft shear seam: long streamlines above, short stubby ones below; a dashed intended glidepath running straight down to the runway threshold; the solid aircraft sitting beneath that dashed path, just after crossing the seam; a pale ghost of the same aircraft still on the dashed path at the same point along final. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Headwind loss on final arrives late in the approach, where you have the least altitude to spare.

On final you are low and committed to a path. The wing knows only the air moving over it right now. Pattern altitude is history. A headwind that weakens as you descend hands you a sink you never asked for.

It is easy to read the sag as your own flying. The air changed. The Airplane Flying Handbook covers this in its approach and landing chapter. The speed does come back. You are lower than you planned by the time it does.
FlightDecide reads the wind lines in your TAF for the planned window, including a low level wind shear group when the forecast carries one.
One sentence worth carrying down final: the speed sagged because the air changed, and the airplane is already going low.
teaches: A decreasing headwind with descent produces a momentary loss of indicated airspeed.
The aircraft sinks below the intended path, and getting the airspeed back does not by itself return it to the path.
The pilot must recover the path, promptly adding power and adjusting pitch to correct for the wind's effect on the descent.
posts.intent: Descending out of a stronger wind into a weaker one costs airspeed, and the aircraft sinks below the path while it recovers.
